The Section on Boundaries, Encompassing the Central and Peripheral Regions and Relics. Part One: The Section on Boundaries of the *Shijia fangzhi*.
This is the realm over which the Buddha reigns,
called the Sahā World;
it was formerly translated as "Saha."
This refers to what is called the "Endurance Land" (Sahā-lokadhātu) in the sūtras;
it means that the people of this land possess strong discernment, power of memory, and mindfulness,
such that they can endure suffering and pleasure and are capable vessels for the Way.
Therefore, it is the realm of the Buddha-King.
According to this boundary, it is encircled by Iron Mountains; beyond these mountains is emptiness, an emptiness that cannot be measured.
Below the earth is the ground; below the ground is gold;
below the gold is water; and below the water is wind.
That wind is more solid and firm than even vajra.
The mental power of sentient beings, induced by their common karma,
is able to sustain the world so that it does not collapse.
Beyond the wind-circle is simply empty space.
Approximately, this circular perimeter ascends from below to the very limit of the formless realm,
which is called the "Peak of Existence" (bhavāgra).
As for its delineated boundary, it extends across a vast distance.
In the end, it cannot be measured by the number of *li*.
Furthermore, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
there is a great stone that falls from the heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Only after eighteen thousand three hundred and eighty-three years does it finally reach the ground.
Taking these upper and lower dimensions as its boundaries,
this is called the sovereign realm of a single Buddha, with the Great Thousandfold Iron Ring Mountains serving as its frontier domain.
2. Section on the Comprehensive Survey of the Records of Śākyamuni’s Region. Section Two on the Comprehensive Survey of the Records of Śākyamuni’s Region:
According to the records, the number of lands encompassed within the Iron Wheel Mountains of the Sahā World is ten trillion.
How is this known? That which we currently inhabit is but a single country,
and each country has its own Mount Sumeru.
This is what is referred to in the sutras as Mount Sumeru.
Situated in the great ocean upon the surface of the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*),
it rises eighty thousand *yojanas* half out of the sea.
The sun and moon revolve around its waist.
It is surrounded on the outside by seven layers of golden mountains,
and within each lies an ocean possessing the eight meritorious qualities.
Beyond that is the Salt Sea, vast and boundless.
Outside the sea is a mountain composed of iron that encircles it on all sides;
within the sea, there are places fit for habitation.
In brief, there are four.
Based on Mount Sumeru, they are divided according to the directions:
the eastern continent is named Videha.
The southern continent is named Jambudvīpa;
the western continent is named Aparagoyānī;
and the northern continent is named Uttarakuru.
These four continents are also called the "four existences" (catvāro bhavāḥ).
They are the dwelling place of humanity and the domain ruled by the Buddha.
By this standard, extending laterally within the Iron Encircling Mountains (Cakravāḍa), there are only these four continents.
Above Mount Sumeru are the twenty-eight heavens;
together with one sun and moon, this constitutes a single world-system.
When such units reach a count of one thousand, it forms [a small chiliocosm].
The area completely surrounded by the Cakravāḍa mountains is called a small thousandfold world system (*sāhasracūḍika lokadhātu*).
When the number of these small thousandfold world systems reaches one thousand,
the area completely surrounded by the Cakravāḍa mountains is called a medium thousandfold world system (*dvisāhasramadhyama lokadhātu*).
When one thousand of these intermediate chiliocosms reaches [the number] one thousand,
surrounded on all sides by the Cakravāḍa mountains, it is called a great trichiliocosm.
According to this, there is a great trichiliocosm.
Within these, from the four continents, the king of mountains, the sun, and the moon,
up to the Summit of Existence (bhavāgra), there are ten trillion locations,
all of which are governed by the Buddha.
All alike follow the teachings of the Voice (Śabda).
**Chapter Three: On the Center and the Borders of Śākyamuni’s Domain** Now, as for the territory governed by the Dharma King, it encompasses all within the Great Trichiliocosm.
If one takes Chengdu as the reference point, this continent is its constant place of residence;
thus, this continent lies in the midst of the ocean south of Mount Sumeru.
Its extent from east to west, traversed by both water and land, is two hundred and forty thousand li.
It is twenty-eight thousand li from north to south.
Furthermore, according to the treatise,
its three sides are equal, each measuring two thousand yojanas.
The southern side measures three and a half yojanas;
thus, it is wide in the north and narrow in the south, resembling the face of a human or an elephant.
Furthermore, this is according to the common records.
The inhabited area of the realm measures one hundred sixteen thousand li from east to west;
its extent from south to north is roughly the same.
As for the capital city, it should be the city of Kapilavastu in the land where the Buddha was born, located at its center.
This means it is situated within the fourfold Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa).
Thus, a sutra states:
"It is the center of three thousand suns and moons, and twelve thousand worlds (lokadhātu)."
By the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, he is not born in the borderlands,
for such lands are tilted; rather,
it is in the Middle Kingdom of Central India, beneath the tree where the Tathāgata attained enlightenment.
There is a Vajrāsana used to support the Buddha;
based on this as the primary argument, its centrality is determined in relation to the rest of the world.
If one were to define the meaning of "center" for this continent (*Jambudvīpa*) itself, it would be clarified by five criteria.
What are called names, regions, times, waters, and people constitute the five [categories].
Regarding what is called "names":
it is universally said that those of the Western Regions consider themselves to be the Central Kingdom (Madhyadeśa).
It is also called the Kingdom of Central India.
This land is known as the next stage after Xiantan-gui;
furthermore, it points toward the western world as the "Middle Kingdom."
If it were not the Middle Way, then the two views of ordinary beings and sages would not be called "middle.
Formerly, during the Song dynasty, there was He Chengtian of Donghai;
he was renowned for his vast learning and ranked among the foremost of the many eminent scholars.
He asked the śramaṇa Huìyán:
"By what calendrical system does the Buddha-land employ to designate it as 'Central'?
Huìyán replied:
In the land of India,
on the day of the summer solstice at midday, there is no shadow;
this is what is called the center of heaven and earth, where all is level.
Because Jing Gui of this country measured the celestial sphere, there were surplus fractions;
consequently, the calendars of the Three Dynasties had both large and small intercalary fractions.
As these were increased or diminished, the accumulated calculations would immediately deviate from the observed phenomena, clearly showing they were not centered on the truth.
Shengtian had no words with which to resist him.
When Emperor Wen heard of this, he issued an edict for Ren Yu to receive [the teachings] from him.
Indeed, as the "Eight Difficulties" indicate, those in the borderlands were not included [among those eligible for ordination].
To emerge from the mundane and enter the sacred, one must first pass through the Middle Kingdom.
Thus, the Great Xia personally received the sounds and forms [of the teachings],
while the Eastern Flower [China] opened its traces of instruction late.
This is indeed the way of principle and number.
Regarding the two mentions of "li" (yojanas):
this continent is divided into three major portions.
Of these two divisions, the northern part is vast and sparsely populated;
it is the dwelling place of the Xiongnu and lacks the capacity for administrative affairs.
The southern division extends as far as the Three Seas.
The people there were for the most part refined and alert, capable of receiving the holy transformation.
Therefore, Dao-sheng established his great sanctuary there.
Thus, Chengguangzi said: [as quoted above].
From the kingdom of Central India to the east lies the kingdom of Zhendan (China)—Zhendan being the designation for the Divine Land—five thousand eight hundred li away.
To the south of that land, according to the people there, lies the kingdom of Jinti five thousand eight hundred li away.
To the west it extends fifty-eight thousand li to the kingdom of Aṅga;
to the north it extends fifty-eight thousand li to Mount Kṣudragandhamādana and Lake Anavatapta.
Contemplating these, one comprehensively grasps its vastness and its limits.
To align them thoroughly so as to establish their central point,
the principle is easily revealed.
As for the three mentions of "timeliness":
That which lies south of the Snowy Mountains is called the Central Land (Madhyadeśa).
It is level and even, with a climate that is temperate throughout both winter and summer;
plants and trees are perpetually flourishing, and frost never falls.
As for the other remote borderlands, what need is there to speak of them?
Regarding the fourth term, "water":
at the center of this continent, there is a great lake.
It is named Anavatapta, which in the language of Tang means "Free from Heat and Torment.
This is what is referred to in the sutras as Lake Anavatapta.
It is situated south of Mount Gandhamādana and north of the Great Snow Mountains.
It dwells upon a mountain peak that is not accessible to ordinary beings.
The lake is eight hundred li in circumference, and its four shores are adorned with jewels.
Directly to the south, on level ground, lies the abode of the hells;
thus, it extends five thousand li to the east of the Vajrāsana.
Furthermore, the lake is situated directly south at the tip of the continent.
To its north lies the Mīra Valley;
it is also situated north of the Thousand Springs on the Pamir Mountains.
Looking upward, its fixed position corresponds approximately to the North Star.
Looking toward the fifth [stage] now, it appears to lean toward the west;
for every one *cun* above corresponds to one thousand *li* below.
Thus, the Thousand Springs (*Qianquan*) are more than eight thousand *li* from the capital.
It measures less than one chi in depth.
To the north of this pond, it is less than a thousand li from the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra;
to the southeast is the kingdom of Kuluṭa.
To the southwest lies the country of Jibin (Kashmir),
each [direction] extending for more than a thousand *li*.
Thus, the four seas constitute the ultimate limit of the flow of the great waters.
Therefore, this single lake branches out into four rivers,
each flowing according to the topography of the land to empty into a respective sea; thus,
to the east of the Pamir Mountains, the waters flow into the Eastern Sea.
To the south of Daxun, waters flow into the Southern Sea;
to the west of the Snowy Mountains, waters flow into the Western Sea;
and to the north of Daqin, waters flow into the Northern Sea.
Therefore, the land is high and the waters naturally flow into its center; this location, situated on the edge of the sea, is known as "Difficult to Take.
Furthermore, the Buddhist scriptures are vast and comprehensive, encompassing all matters;
having seen widely into the meanings of the sages and worthies, they are not false or superficial.
All that has been listed above accords with the maps;
however, among the books and histories produced in this Divine Land (China),
there is an extreme abundance of allegories, conjectures, and frivolous exaggerations.
At this point, I shall further expand upon this category by drawing from the Buddhist scriptures;
these are all utterly corrupt, so I shall cite them for you.
The *Shui jing* (Classic of Water) states:
The Hill of No Heat (Anavatapta) is Mount Kunlun; furthermore, the *Fu-nan zhuan* states that Mount Anavatapta is Mount Kunlun; and the *Shanhai jing* also says:
To the south of the banks of the Flowing Sands,
behind the Red Water and in front of the Black Water,
there is a great mountain named Mount Kunlun. It is also said:
Six hundred li to the west of Mount Zhong,
there is Mount Kunlun, from which five waters emerge. According to the *Mu Tianzi Zhuan*, the pronunciation of Mount Chong is the same as that of Mount Zhong.
It is further stated:
"Within the seas lies Mount Kunlun,
situated in the northwest beneath the Sovereign."
It is eight hundred *fang* square and ten thousand *gen* high.
Furthermore, the *Shizhou ji* states:
"Mount Kunlun Ling is Mount Kun."
The Hai region of the Northern Sea is located one hundred and thirty thousand *li* from the shore;
this refers approximately to Mount Sumeru as described in the Buddhist scriptures.
Furthermore, there is a mountain named Fangzhang in the Eastern Sea.
It is also called Kunlun. Furthermore,
it is said that the Queen Mother of the West told King Mu of Zhou:
The mountain is thirty-six myriad *li* from Xianyang;
its height above the level ground is thirty-six thousand *li*.
Furthermore, the *Zhou Mu Wang Zhuan* (Biography of King Mu of Zhou) describes the Queen Mother of the West as follows:
From the capital of Zhou to the rivers Chan and Jian, it is eleven thousand one hundred li. (Shenyijing).
On Mount Kunlun there is a bronze pillar;
its height reaches into heaven, and its circumference is three thousand li.
Rong’s commentary states:
"Twelve thousand li southeast of Mount Kunlun on Zhuzhou lies Mount Wuwai. The *Shiji* states:
"Mount Kunlun is fifty thousand li from Mount Songgao and ten thousand one hundred li high. Guo Pu says: [as cited above].

It is over two thousand five hundred *li* high; according to the *Huainanzi*, it is ten thousand one hundred *li*, fourteen paces, and two feet six inches high; the *Daojing Zaoli Tiandi Ji* (Record of the Establishment of Heaven and Earth in the Daoist Canon) states:
Mount Kunlun is four thousand eight hundred li high.
The *Zhuanxing jiku jing* (Sutra on Transforming Form to Relieve Suffering) states that it is ten thousand nine thousand li high.
It is further said that this mountain floats;
it is also said to be thirty li south of Mount Kunlun.
There are successively a thousand Mount Kunluns,
which is called a small chiliocosm.
The *Huahu jing* says:
Mount Kunlun is ninefold in height;
the distances between its peaks are each nine thousand li.
It is also said that it is ten million five thousand li high.
Regarding the two preceding traditions of Confucianism and Daoism,
although their physical dimensions differ, they do not extend beyond Mount Kunlun;
one must seek Mount Kunlun as the nearest mountain.
Thus, the region of Jiuquan in Xiliang was the place where Empress Mu beheld the Queen Mother of the West;
this is detailed in their maps and records.
If one speaks of the distant Kunlun Mountains,
they lie between Mount Gandhamādana and the Snowy Mountains (Himavat),
from which the source of the River originates.
Therefore, the *Erya* says:
"The River issues from the Kunlun ruins.
Guo Pu’s *Tuzan* (Illustrated Eulogy) states:
The three tiers of Mount Kunlun are called the Pillar of Heaven;
it is truly the numinous repository of the River Source.
According to the *Yugong*, it says:
Regarding the statement that the Yellow River is led from Jishi, this is merely a designation based on the location where the submerged current emerges.
If one investigates its true source, there is indeed a basis for it; thus, a Buddhist scripture says:
To the east of this Lake Anavatapta,
there is a silver ox-mouth from which the Gaṅgā River issues;
this is what was formerly called the Ganges.
Circumambulating the lake to the right, it flows into the southeastern sea.
To the south is a golden elephant from whose mouth issues the Indus River,
which is the ancient Sindhu River.
Circumambulating the lake to the right, it flows into the southwestern ocean.
To the west is a horse-mouth made of lapis lazuli from which the Vakṣu River emerges;
this is the ancient Bactrus River.
Circling the lake as described above, it enters the northwest sea.
To the north is a crystal lion’s mouth from which the Sītā River flows;
this is the ancient Śītā River.
As described above, one circumambulates the pond and enters the eastern sea.
According to the *Hetu* (River Chart),
five thousand li to the east of Mount Kunlun is named Zhongshou (the Central Divine Land).
It is also called Chixian. Furthermore, according to the *Shu* (Book of Documents), it says:
"The source of the River flows out from the northeast of the Congling Mountains into the Qisha Valley."
It divides into two streams;
the northeastern branch flows south of the Southern Mountains of Khotan and emerges from the northwest of the kingdom.
It then flows eastward as a great river, passing to the southeast of the city of Kāpiśī.
Furthermore, traveling west from the kingdom of Shule,
and then northeast to the foot of a city,
one proceeds south for over five hundred *li* from the kingdom of Huiluo to reach the southern border of the kingdom of Wushai.
Proceeding again northeast for six hundred and ten li, one reaches the city of Chigou (Red Valley) on the border of the Wusun kingdom to the north of the country of Shule.
Continuing east for two hundred and seventy li, one passes to the south of the country of Gumu.
Traveling further east for six hundred and seventy li, one passes to the south of the kingdom of Kucha.
Continuing east for three hundred and fifty li, one passes to the south of the kingdom of Wulei;
this was the seat of the Protector-General during the Han dynasty.
It is 2,110 li to the southwest of Shule.
It is 1,785 li to the southeast of the kingdom of Shan-shan.
Four hundred *li* to the northeast of the kingdom of Uḍḍiyāna,
the river flows again three hundred and forty *li* to the southeast, passing south of the kingdom of Kharalika.
It then flows another two hundred and forty *li* to the east, passing south of the kingdom of Kṛṣṇagiri.
From here, traveling east for two thousand six hundred and sixty *li*, one reaches the Yumen Pass.
The river flows further east through Liánchéng and empties into Bīnchéng; north of Qiémò State, it joins the Zhī River.
The river flows again to the east through the territory of Loulan.
Continuing further east, it passes south of the city of the kingdom of Shanshan and,
after traveling several hundred li to the northeast, enters the Lop Nor (Pu-chang Hai).
To the east of this sea, slightly to the north, it is one thousand three hundred *li* from Yumen;
further to the northeast, it is three hundred *li* from Yangguan.
This river flows underground southward and slightly westward for several thousand *li* within the Pochang Sea.
The entry into Mount Jishi is located within the Qiang region at Shao-dang.
The records state that Jishi is distant from Mount Kunlun.
It is one thousand seven hundred and forty *li*.
Some say that it flows underground for thirteen thousand *li*.
These various speculative theories are difficult to investigate and verify in detail.
The river originates from Mount Jishi and flows southwest for nine bends;
it then flows northeast to join with other streams through the territory of Xizhi, forming what is known as the "River Bend" (Hexi).
Furthermore, turning northeast and entering the frontier barriers,
one passes south of Zhang Sai in Dunhuang;
this is the source of the Yellow River.
According to this veritable record, in tracing the source of the river,
one must reach the Anavatapta Lake (Wu re chi) before the investigation can be considered exhaustive.
However, the abode of this lake deity is beyond the reach of humans;
furthermore, it lies within the region of the Snowy Mountains in Northern India,
bordering the Central Land where the Buddha was born to the south.
Because its location is high and superior, it is not a peripheral realm.
The fifth refers to "humans," which includes neither the ordinary nor the sages.
The ultimate rank of ordinary beings is called that of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin);
the ultimate rank of sages is called that of a Dharma King (dharmarāja).
Indeed, these two kings, were they not to be born, would simply not exist.
Those born there must necessarily dwell in the center.
Furthermore, mountains, rivers, nations, and towns are the objects of reliance and retribution for people;
when the people are superior, their environment becomes superior.
Therefore, these two kings reside there.
Furthermore, regarding the four types of wheel-turning kings who rule over the four continents,
the one with the golden wheel possesses all four [possessions].
The silver wheel [ruler] excludes one continent, the north;
the copper wheel [ruler] excludes two directions, the northwest;
the iron wheel [ruler] is in the south, excluding the three realms of existence.
As for the term "Jambudvīpa," it is the Central Indic (Madhyadeśa) pronunciation;
in the language of Tang, it is translated as "the abode of the Wheel-Turning King."
Regarding the universal or restricted application of the four wheel-turning kings,
this is a distinction found specifically in the Southern Continent;
in ancient translations, this continent was rendered as [Jambudvīpa].
It is called "Excellent Golden Land.
This refers to Jāmbūnada gold,
which is found in the ocean off the northern shore of the continent.
Golden light floated out over the sea.
Beside it was a grove of Jambū trees whose fruits were exceedingly large;
only those who had attained supernatural powers could reach that place.
Now, regarding the title "Wheel-Turning King" (Cakravartin) for this continent, two conditions must be met.
Furthermore, this continent is governed by four lords:
the region south of the Snowy Mountains (Himavat) extending to the Southern Ocean is known as the Domain of the Elephant Lord.
The land is characterized by heat and humidity, making it particularly suitable for elephants to dwell;
thus, the king maintains his kingdom with an elephant army.
The local customs are impetuous and fierce, and the people are devoted to the study of various arts.
This is the country of India.
However, the name "India" is sometimes called "Xian-dou" (Sindhu).
Some call it Tianzhu;
some call it Shendu; others call it Tiandu, and so forth.
These are all merely erroneous and deviant transmissions.
However, India is taken as the standard; there was no way to translate [the original] into Chinese during the Tang dynasty.
To the west of the Snowy Mountains, reaching as far as the Western Sea, is the land known as Baozhu (Lord of Jewels).
Its territory borders the Western Sea and abounds in rare treasures;
its people show little regard for ritual propriety but place great value on wealth, and thus it is considered a Hu kingdom.
North of the Snowy Mountains and reaching as far as the Northern Sea, the land is cold and suitable for horses; it is known as the Land of the Lord of Horses.
Its customs are fierce and violent, its people are accustomed to killing, and they wear animal skins and furs.
This is the country of the Turks.
From east of the Snow Mountains to the Eastern Sea, they are known as the lords of men.
The land is harmonious and pleasant, and its customs practice benevolence and righteousness.
The people of the land of Cīna cherish their native soil and loathe relocation;
this is the very country formerly known as Zhendan.
The four sovereigns mentioned above ruled over a single continent.
The realms are divided and kings rule according to their respective continents;
it has been established from antiquity that a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) resides at the center while other kings dwell at the periphery, a fact that remains unchanged through the ages.
Yet, the scholars of this land remain mired in the teachings of Confucius.
Taking this as the center, all else is subsumed under the periphery;
specifically designating Luoyang as the Middle Kingdom (Zhongguo) was based on the system of the Five Sacred Peaks established by the Yellow Emperor (Xuanyuan).
This is not yet a comprehensive and grand perspective.
Furthermore, you categorize Western Tibet as a "barbarian" (hu) country;
however, it was there that the Buddha was born and traveled.
To the south of the Snowy Mountains lies the land known as the Kingdom of the Brahmins.
It is isolated from the Hu (barbarians) and their scripts and languages differ;
therefore, the various Brahmins of the Five Indias [are distinct].
Script is the script of heaven, and speech is the speech of heaven.
It is said that at the beginning of the kalpa, when it was first formed, Brahmā descended;
because of the flavor of the earth’s fatness, human beings came into being.
Since the celestial dharma of the primordial language and script has never been interrupted,
those who worship the deities according to their customs are numerous;
this is because their births have specific causes.
The Hu people, being Western barbarians, have no tradition of the Way or its arts.

Their written language and speech are transmitted and understood only through separate national records and translations. As for the written language and speech that originate from the Divine Land (China), they have no original source [among them].
Furthermore, written records can be sought through their practical applications.
Fuxi established the eight trigrams, which Wenwang later doubled;
as for Cangjie’s bird-track script, its forms were not widely practiced.
In the Han dynasty, Xu Shen had just produced the *Shuowen*,
in which characters numbered only nine thousand and were arranged by category;
now, as they gradually permeate the world, written texts number thirty thousand.
This arises according to the intentions of individuals and the requirements of the times;
it does not compare with the fixed nature of the scripts and languages of the Five Indias.
Above, there are five meanings.
By means of the center and the boundaries of meditative concentration, one may reflect upon all things.
The rest is as described in the *Record of Sacred Sites* by the Śramaṇa Lingyu of Wei Commandery during the early Sui dynasty.

4. Section on Historical Sites from the *Shijia fangzhi* (Record of the Regions of Śākyamuni), Part Four. From the Han to the Tang dynasties, those who traveled to India were so numerous that their paths cannot be fully recounted.
As recorded below, according to the records of the Great Tang,
there were formerly three routes for envoys.
Following the route of my journey, I have fully observed the various sites left behind;
I shall now arrange them in sequence.
As for the eastern route, it proceeds from the northwest of Hezhou.
Crossing the great river, one ascends Mount Mantianling;
after traveling less than four hundred li, one reaches Shanzhou.
Further west for less than a hundred li, one arrives at Shancheng.
This is the site of the ancient town of Guzhuo.
Traveling southwest for another hundred *li*,
one reaches the former Chengfeng Garrison, which was the site of the Sui dynasty's border market.
Traveling further west for less than two hundred li,
one reaches Qinghai.
In the midst of the sea is a small mountain.
The sea is over seven hundred *li* in circumference.
To the southwest of the sea lies the headquarters of the Tuyuhun;
further southwest is the border of the state known as the Bailan Qiang.
To the north, it reaches the city of Jiyu;
to the northwest, it reaches the country of Dami;
and further to the southwest, it reaches the country of Suvī.
Proceeding further southwest, one arrives at the kingdom of Gan.
Continuing southward with a slight turn to the east, one reaches the kingdom of Tibet (Tufan).
Further southwest, one arrives at the kingdom of Xiaoyangtong.
Furthermore, traveling southwest across the Da-cang Pass, one reaches the southern border of Tibet.
Continuing slightly southeast across the Ma-shang Pass,
one enters the valley at the San-bi Pass.
Passing through thirteen ladders and nineteen plank paths,
one proceeds either southeast or southwest,
climbing along rattan vines and grasping creeping tendrils.

Traveling on foot for over forty days, he arrived at the kingdom of Nepal in North India; this territory borders Tibet and measures approximately nine thousand *li* in extent, with the capital situated in its center.
Traveling over one hundred li east from Shanzhou,
and proceeding northward for another six hundred li, one arrives at Liangzhou.
It lies two thousand li to the east of the capital.
From Liangxi, traveling four hundred and seventy li slightly to the north, one reaches Ganzhou.
From there, traveling another four hundred li to the west, one reaches Suzhou.
From there, traveling seven thousand five li to the west and slightly to the north, one arrives [at the destination].
He arrived at the ancient Yumen Pass.
The pass lies between the northern and southern mountains.
Traveling further west for four hundred li less, he reached Guazhou.
Traveling again southwest for more than three hundred li across the desert, one reaches Shazhou.
Continuing southwest for more than seven hundred li across the desert, one arrives at the ancient kingdom of Navapa, which is the territory of Loulan and is also called Shan-shan.
Traveling again southwest for over a thousand *li*, one arrives at the ancient kingdom of Śimadhāna,
which is the same as Jamludvīpa.
Traveling further west for over six hundred *li*, one arrives at the ancient kingdom of Tura.
All are but desolate cities.
Again, traveling westward into the great shifting sands for over four hundred li,
one reaches the eastern border of the kingdom of Gostana, which is the country called Yutian in the Chinese histories.
The seat of the Protector-General is a Chinese military outpost.
To the east, it is nine thousand six hundred and seventy li from Chang’an; its pass is named Niran-cheng, and the local people call their land the Kingdom of Yudun.
It is over four thousand li in circuit;
more than half of its area consists of sandy deserts.
There are over one hundred monasteries, with five thousand monks who are scholars of the Mahāyāna.
From the pass to the Hemo River is over two hundred li.
In the city of Jimo, there is a standing sandalwood image more than twenty feet high,
which manifests numerous miraculous signs and radiates brilliant light.
Those who were ill would recover as soon as they applied gold leaf to the image according to the location of their pain.
This image was originally located in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī;
it was created by King Udayana.
Flying through the air, he arrived at this country.
To the north of the city of Haluluka, there was an extraordinary arhat whom he went to pay his respects every day.
The king, initially disbelieving, threw sand and dust upon the arhat.
He then told those who were devoted and faithful:
"Seven days from now, sand and dust shall fill the city."
On the following two days, it rained jewels that filled the streets.
On the night of the seventh day, as expected, it rained earth that filled the city until hardly anyone remained.
The one who had previously been informed dug a pit in the ground beforehand and emerged through the hole;
he went eastward toward the Jīmūtavāhana image, and the others arrived there as well.
An annotation states that when the Dharma was about to perish, the image entered the Dragon Palace.
As for the city of Hela, it has now become a great mound; should King Daibai (Mahābala) wish to excavate treasures there, he will inevitably encounter a wind-disaster.
Furthermore, traveling three hundred and thirty *li* west from the city of Śrīmaṣṭhāna,
one arrives at the capital city of the kingdom.
Ten *li* to the south is a great monastery established by a former king.
More than ten li to the southwest, there is a temple containing a standing image made of lacquered cloth.
It came from the kingdom of Kucha.
Formerly, a subject of this country paid his respects to it there.
The minister returned to his native country and remembered [the image] incessantly;
the image then arrived there one night, whereupon he donated his residence to establish a monastery.
This was at the city of Bālkh, more than three hundred li to the west of the capital.
There is a seated image seven feet high, whose marks and signs of excellence are peerless;
a jeweled crown upon its head occasionally manifests radiance.
It is located one hundred and sixty li west of the capital city.
On the great desert sands along the road, there was only a mound of rat droppings, as large as a hedgehog and golden-silver in color.
Formerly, when the Xiongnu came to invade, the King prayed to the spirit of the rats; consequently, they bit people and horses during the night.
The weapons broke and shattered, and they naturally retreated.
About five li west of the capital city, there is a temple with a stupa over one hundred feet high, which frequently manifests radiant signs;
the King was moved by it and obtained several hundred grains of śarīra relics.
The Arhat raised the stupa with his right hand and placed it within the casket;
he then lowered it down without it tilting or shaking.

More than ten *li* to the southwest of the capital city lies Mount Gośṛṅga, which in this language means "Ox Horn. There is a monastery there where an image manifested radiance; the Buddha once visited this place to preach the Dharma for devas and humans.
It is recorded that this kingdom was established with a high regard for the Mahāyāna teachings.
In a mountain cave within a rocky chamber dwells an arhat who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), awaiting the advent of Maitreya Buddha.
Several hundred years ago, a cliff collapsed and blocked the entrance.
Its southern border adjoins the kingdom of Dongnu (Eastern Women).
From the city of the kingdom, one crosses mountains and valleys to the west.

After traveling more than eight hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Jiegujia (Juzhu), which constitutes the southern border [of the previous territory]. This kingdom is over one thousand *li* in circuit;
it contains some ten Buddhist temples with more than a hundred monks.
For those who study the Mahāyāna,
there is a mountain to the south of the kingdom where a Tārā stūpa stands; there,
pines and streams flow luxuriantly, and stone chambers are deep and pure.
There were three arhats who had entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*);
their hair and beards grew constantly, so the monks shaved them regularly.
Among the monks of the five regions of India, there were those who had realized the fruits of the path.
Many reside in this chamber.
Furthermore, traveling north for three hundred *li*, one reaches the capital city.
It is over ten *li* in circumference, with mountains and hills stretching continuously, bordered by two rivers.
Furthermore, to the northwest of the kingdom,
crossing the Sindhu River at the top of the Great Sand Ridge and traveling over five hundred li, one arrives.
The Kingdom of Khasha is Shule (Kashgar). It is over five thousand *li* in circuit, with several hundred monasteries and tens of thousands of monks.
They practice the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna.
The land is mostly rocky and desert; as for its customs, when children are born, their heads are pressed flat.
From here, traveling south through mountains, wilds,
and stony plateaus for over five hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Wu-she (Uḍḍiyāna).
The territory extends for over one thousand *li*, and the capital city is over ten *li* in circuit.
It borders the Sindhu River to the south and adheres to the Buddha-dharma.
There are more than ten monasteries with fewer than a thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
More than two hundred li west of the city, one reaches a great mountain.
There is a stupa upon its ridge;
several hundred years ago, the mountain cliff collapsed of its own accord.
Among them was a bhikṣu sitting with his eyes closed;
his form was exceedingly grand, and his beard and hair hung down,
covering his shoulders and face.
The king poured clarified butter over him and struck the ghaṇṭā;
the bhikṣu looked up and said,
"My teacher is Kāśyapa."
"Now I have finally heard that he has already entered parinirvāṇa.
He further asked whether Śākyamuni Buddha had appeared in the world,
to which he replied, "He has already passed into extinction."
He immediately ascended into the air and transformed himself into fire to cremate his body.
From that land, white jasper, blue jade, and other minerals were produced.
Crossing the river west of the city of the kingdom, he ascended the Pamir Mountains (Congling).
Traveling eastward from Donggang for over eight hundred *li*, one reaches Fusha.
This site lies amidst four mountains and covers an area of over a hundred *qing*.
It is devoid of trees, possessing only sparse grasses.
The circumstances are as explained elsewhere.
Furthermore, traveling southwest across a great mountain range,
one arrives at the kingdom of Kāpiśī.
It is over two thousand *li* in circuit, and its capital city is over fifty *li* in circumference.
It borders the Sindhu River to the north and reveres the Buddha-dharma.
There are more than ten monasteries with over five hundred monks.
The people belong to the Hinayana Sarvastivada school.
To the southeast of the country are two large stone caves, each with one entrance;
in each, an Arhat has entered the meditative concentration of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
After more than seven hundred years had passed,
his beard and hair grew anew each year, and he shaved them separately for each year.
Furthermore, traveling northwest for over three hundred li:
Upon reaching the royal capital,
one encounters the Tīrtha mountain range to the southeast, with its ridges extending in continuous succession;
then, turning slightly southwest, one ascends the mountain.
After traveling over five hundred li through ice and snow, one reaches the Pamir River Valley (Pamīra-kulyā).
It extends over a thousand li from east to west and more than a hundred li from south to north;
in some places it is so narrow that it does not exceed ten li.
Located between the Great Snow Mountains of the north and south,
the land is saline and alkaline with many stones;
vegetation is sparse and there are no human inhabitants.
South of the river and beyond the mountains lies the kingdom of Bolor.
This river flows from atop the Great Onion Range (Pamir),
which is the highest point of land on the continent of Jambudvīpa.
Within it is a great dragon pool,
measuring over three hundred li from east to west and over fifty li from south to north; from it emerge large eggs.
That river flows westward until it reaches the eastern border of the kingdom of Dharmasthiti, where it joins the Vakṣu River;
from this point westward, all waters flow west,
while one stream branches off to the east.
To the northeast, it reaches the western border of the kingdom of Khasa and joins with the Sindhu River;
from this point onward, all these waters flow eastward.
The Dragon Pond lies directly south of Anavatapta Lake;
to its north is the Thousand Springs River,
and to its south is Daitai Ridge.
It is named Varṣika, extending three or four hundred *li* from south to north;
the mountains and terrain are exceedingly high.
To the north of the lake is Mount Dàcōng (Great Onion).
The *Shui jing* (Classic of Waters) states that it is over a thousand *li* in height and gradually slopes downward on both sides.
The ridges running north to south are extremely numerous, numbering more than a hundred;
as many of them are lush with mountain leeks and possess steep,
verdant cliffs, they are named accordingly.
Lingnan borders the Great Snow Mountains to the south and reaches Qianquan to the north;
it is approximately two thousand five hundred li in extent.
To the east it reaches Wushai, and to the west it extends to the kingdom of Dahuok;
it spans approximately three thousand li.
Furthermore, from the southwest of the valley, one enters the mountainous wilderness.
After traveling more than seven hundred *li*,
one arrives at the country of Śāmbī.
It is two thousand six hundred *li* in circuit.
The soil produces realgar, and the people believe in Buddhism; there are two temples, and the monks are few.
To the north, one crosses Mount Dharmaṣṭhita, a great rocky mountain, and arrives.
The country of Śrīkṣetra is over two thousand li in circuit; its mountains and desert wastes stretch across the plains.
Furthermore, one crosses rivers and mountains to the south.
Upon reaching the country of Dardastīn, also known as the Kingdom of Pōkàn or the Kingdom of Hùmì, this is the ancient territory of Tukhāra;
it lies between two mountains.
It is fifteen hundred li from east to west and slightly less than one hundred li from south to north;
in some places it is so narrow that it does not exceed one li.
To the east it borders the Varku River.
There are more than ten monks in the monastery, which is relatively few in number.
Above the stone image in the city monastery—
A circular canopy of gold and copper, adorned with various jewels, was suspended above;
when people circumambulated it, the canopy would turn accordingly,
and when they stopped, it would stop as well.
The stone walls surrounding it were unfathomable in their nature.
Some said it was due to the power of a sage;
others claimed it was the secret of a mechanical device.
Furthermore, traveling southwest by climbing mountains and entering valleys for over five hundred li,
one arrives at the country of Kulūta, which is also an ancient land.
It is over two thousand li in circuit, and there are few who have faith or inclination [toward the Dharma].
Furthermore, traveling northwest across the mountain ridges for more than three hundred li,
one arrives at...
The country of Yintubo (Yinbuke) is also an ancient territory.
It is over one thousand *li* in circuit, and its capital city is more than ten *li* in circumference.
Traveling further northwest through mountain valleys for over two hundred *li*, one arrives [at the next destination].
Upon arrival,
[he reached] the kingdom of Badakshan (Bodakṣana), which is also an ancient land.
It is over two thousand li in circuit.
The mountain cliffs surrounding the capital city measure sixty or seventy *li* in circumference;
there are four monasteries there, and the monks are few in number.
Traveling westward from the valley for more than two hundred *li*:
Upon arrival,
he found that the country of Himatala was also his former territory;
it is over three thousand li in circuit, with mountains and rivers interspersed.
There were several dozen fortified cities.
To the west, one crossed over mountains and valleys for more than three hundred li until reaching [the destination].
The kingdom of Kṛśma is also an ancient territory.
It is over ten *li* from east to west and three hundred *li* from south to north.
The capital city is fifteen *li* in circuit.
To the north lies the kingdom of Parika, which is also an ancient territory.
It is over one hundred li in width and more than three hundred li from south to north.
The capital city is over twenty li in circuit.
Furthermore, from the country of Kṛṣṇa, one crosses steep heights and enters a valley;
after traveling more than three hundred li through the riverine plains, one arrives [at the destination].
The kingdom of Mengjian is also an ancient site;
it is over four hundred li in circuit, and its capital city is sixteen li in circuit.
Crossing the river to the north, one reaches the kingdom of A-li-ni, which is likewise an ancient site.
It extends for over three hundred *li* along both banks of the Bāhū River.
The great city is fifteen *li* in circuit.
Crossing the river to the east, one reaches the kingdom of Aḍakāva, which is also an ancient site.
It borders the Former River to the north and is over two hundred li in circuit.
The great city is fifteen li in circuit.
Furthermore, traveling west from the country of Mengjian for more than one hundred li, one reaches [this place].
It lies at the western end of the Pamir Mountains; descending the mountains, one arrives at the country of Huo, which is also an ancient territory.
It is over two thousand li in circuit, and the royal city is over twenty li in circumference.
Its king is a Turk. Most of the small kingdoms south of the Iron Gate are subject to the Turks;
the land is level and peaceful, and the local customs are largely Buddhist.
The monastery had more than ten monks, numbering several hundred;
they studied both the Mahayana and Hinayana teachings.
To the west, one arrives at...
The country of Bāhlika is four or five hundred *li* away.
Traveling southeast across mountains and valleys for more than three hundred *li*,
one reaches the country of Khost (Kauśāmbī), which is also an ancient land.
The kingdom is about one thousand *li* in circumference, with its capital city measuring over ten *li*.
The mountains are many and the rivers narrow; it is extremely windy and cold.
There are three monasteries, and the community of monks is small.
Traveling southeast into a valley, crossing ridges and passing through more than four hundred small towns for over four hundred li,
one arrives at the country of Andarab, which is likewise an ancient land.
It is over three thousand li in circuit.
The royal city is fifteen li in circuit and belongs to the Turks.
There are three monasteries with several dozen monks.
There is a stupa for the Prince of Yü.
The mountain ridges are continuous and extremely cold and harsh.
From here, one ascends southwest toward the Great Snow Mountains,
reaching the eastern end of the Vārṣika Ridge.
After traveling for three days, they again reached the summit,
from which one could see all of Jambudvīpa at once;
all the surrounding mountains sloped downward on all four sides.
Furthermore, following the ridges downward for another three days,
they crossed extremely steep and winding valleys by hacking through ice.
To the west, they passed through dozens of small towns and border cities of the kingdom of Kāpiśī.
Traveling another several hundred li to the southwest, one reaches the royal capital.
Proceeding further west and slightly south for one thousand three hundred li,
crossing mountains and rivers, one arrives at the kingdom of Vṛjiṣṭhāna.
It is over two thousand li in width and over one thousand li from north to south.
The royal city is more than twenty li in circuit, and its inhabitants believe in the Buddha-dharma.
From here, traveling south for over five hundred li, one arrives at [the next destination].
The country of Cōḷa, also called Zāolì, is over seven thousand *li* in circuit; its royal city is over thirty *li* in circuit.
Mountains and rivers are interspersed, and there are several hundred monasteries.
The monastic community numbers in the tens of thousands, all of whom study the Mahāyāna.
There are ten stūpas of King Aśoka and several dozen deva temples, the majority of which belong to non-Buddhists.
The soil is suitable for saffron and fragrant grasses;
it produces *kṣuraka* grass and grows *rāma* grass.
It lies south of the Indus River, at Mount Cakravāḍa.
More than two thousand li to the southeast of the royal city,
one arrives at the kingdom of Varendra in Western India; here,
the northern route merges with the southern path leading toward the Land of the Buddha.
As for the northern route into India:
traveling northwest from the capital for more than three thousand three hundred *li*, one reaches Gua Prefecture (*Guazhou*).
Continuing northwest for another three hundred-odd *li*, one arrives at the mouth of the Moheyan Desert (*Moheyanyiqi*).
Furthermore, traveling northwest for more than eight hundred *li*, one crosses a desert and reaches Rouyuan County.
Continuing southwest for one hundred and sixty *li*, one arrives at Yizhou.
Proceeding west for more than seven hundred *li*, one reaches Puchang County.
Traveling another hundred-odd li to the west, one reaches Xizhou,
which is the former site of Gaochang.
It was the seat of the Commandant of Yihuo during the Han dynasty.
Later, the Juqu ruler of Liang took refuge there during a period of displacement;
it is now within the borderlands.
Furthermore, traveling more than seven hundred li to the west, one arrives at [the next location].
The kingdom of Agni, that is, Uḍḍiyāna, is over six hundred li from east to west and over four hundred li from south to north.
Its capital city is seven or eight li in circuit.
There are more than ten monasteries with over two thousand people,
all of whom study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna.
They were diligent in their observance of the precepts and consumed the three kinds of pure meat.
From this point onward, the Hu tribes became divided;
they valued wealth and slighted righteousness, lacked propriety and respect, and held women in high esteem while degrading men, treating the noble and the lowly as equals.
They established a system of dress in which white was used for auspicious occasions and black for inauspicious ones.
Traveling further southwest for more than two hundred li,
they crossed a small mountain and traversed two great rivers.

Traveling by river for more than seven hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Kujū (pronounced with a retroflex *j* and *wù* reversed), which is Quci. It is over one thousand *li* from east to west and six hundred *li* from south to north.
The city wall is seventeen or eighteen *li* in circumference.
The monastery has more than one hundred monks and over five thousand laypeople;
they all study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna.
As mentioned above, these three groups are pure in their conduct and possess great faith in the Buddha.
In the royal capital, there are numerous shrines and stūpas erected within the private residences of the people, beyond all counting.
In a great city on the eastern border, there is a deva-temple where the nāgas of the pond occasionally emerge.
By mating with mares, they produce dragon colts;
though these newborns are fierce and unruly, they soon become docile for harnessing.
Thus, the kingdom abounds in excellent horses.
There was a king named Golden Flower who was moved by a dragon that served as his mount;
when the king was about to die, the dragon touched his ear with its whip, whereupon it immediately vanished into hiding.
He had illicit relations with another man’s wife and fathered a son who was valiant and fierce.
Because the King [of China] instigated the Tujue to slaughter the people of this city, it has remained desolate and uninhabited.
Over forty li to the north of the city is the East Zhaohuli Temple.
In the Buddha hall there is a jade stone, two feet square,
upon which are the footprints of the Buddha;
they are eighteen inches long and six inches wide.
On fast days, they emit light.
To the left and right of the road outside the western gate of the royal city,
there are standing Buddhas, each over ninety feet in height.
A site was established here where an assembly is held every five years.
To the west is the Aśokārāma Monastery (translated into Chinese as Qite, meaning "Extraordinary").
Formerly, when the King went abroad on a tour, he visited and paid homage to this sacred site.
The younger brother of the mother remained behind as a guardian; fearing slanderous intrigues, he castrated himself.
The King was deeply amazed by this. Later, when the brother encountered someone castrating five hundred oxen, he took pity on them and ransomed them.
By the power of his roots of goodness, a male form suddenly appeared, and he consequently did not enter the palace.
The King, marvelling at this extraordinary event, established a monastery there.
Furthermore, traveling west for over six hundred li across a small desert, one arrives [at the next destination].
The kingdom of Baluka was formerly known by the clan name Mo, also called Hanmo; it is over six hundred li from east to west and over three hundred li from south to north.
The royal city is fifty li in circuit.
There were several dozen monasteries with over a thousand monks, all of whom studied the Hinayana.
Traveling northwest for more than three hundred li,
he crossed a stony desert and reached Mount Ling.
This is the northern plain of the Pamir Mountains (Congling).
Most of the waters flow eastward.
On this road, one must not wear red garments, carry gourds, or raise one's voice in shouting.
Those who commit offenses are blown away by the dragons' winds or buried in sand;
those encountered are invariably submerged.

Traveling westward from here for more than four hundred li, one reaches the Great Clear Lake, also known as the Hot Sea and the Salt Sea, which is over one thousand li in circumference and elongated from east to west.
On all four sides there are mountains where travelers go to offer prayers for blessings.
Furthermore, traveling over five hundred li to the northwest, one reaches the city of Suyab.
It is six or seven li in circuit, and merchants and Hu people dwell there together.
To the west, several dozen isolated cities were likewise situated.
Traveling further west for over four hundred li, one reaches Thousand Springs (Qianquan).
The springs gush forth profusely, covering an area of more than two hundred li square.
To the south lies the Snowy Mountains, with three sides bordering level plains.
Traveling west for one hundred and fifty *li*, one reaches the city of Tālaśī.
Continuing southwest for more than two hundred *li*, one arrives at the city of Gauri.
Traveling another fifty *li* to the south,
one arrives at the ancient kingdom of Chujiàn (Nunu-gu).
It is over one thousand *li* in circuit.

Traveling further west for more than two hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Zhashi (known in the language of Tang as Shiguo), which is over one thousand li in circuit and borders the Ye River to the west.
Continuing southeast for more than one thousand li, one arrives at the kingdom of Poluoshihan.
It is over four thousand *li* in circuit, with mountains surrounding its four borders.
Traveling further west for more than one thousand *li*, one reaches the kingdom of Sthūleśvara.
It is one thousand four hundred *li* in circuit and borders the Ye River to the east.
The River Ye flows from the north of the Pamir Mountains;
flowing northwest and then further northwest, it enters the Great Desert.

It should reach the Kingdom of Samarkand (which in the language of Tang means "Kangguo") after traveling over five hundred *li*. This kingdom is sixteen hundred *li* in circuit and is narrow from north to south.
The capital city is twenty-odd *li* in circuit and is situated in an extremely险固 (precipitous and secure) location.
From here, traveling southeast, one reaches the kingdom of Mi-mo-he (Mi-mo-ha), which is the country of Mīr; it is four or five hundred *li* in circuit and narrow from east to west.
Proceeding further northwest, one reaches the country of Kapitha (曹國), which is approximately one thousand four or five hundred *li* in circuit and is long from east to west.
Traveling another three hundred-odd *li* to the west, one arrives at the country of Kustana (何國), whose circuit is the same as that of Cao, though it is narrow from east to west.
Traveling further west for more than two hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Kāpiśī (formerly known as Anduōguó). It is over one thousand li in circuit.

Traveling further west for more than four hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Bamiyān (formerly known as Bùhánguó). It is over one thousand seven hundred li in circuit and is elongated from east to west.
Traveling further west for more than four hundred *li*, one reaches the kingdom of Fadi (modern-day Xi'an), which is over four hundred *li* in circuit.
Continuing southwest for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Huoli-ximi.
The two banks of the Śubhavastu River extend approximately thirty *li* from east to west and over five hundred *li* from north to south.
Furthermore, one travels southwest from the kingdom of Sāmbhī.
After traveling more than three hundred *li*,
one arrives at the country of Kāśmīra (known as Shiguó), which is approximately fifteen hundred *li* in circuit.
Traveling further southwest for more than two hundred *li*, one enters a great mountain range.
The mountain roads were extremely perilous and sparsely populated.
Traveling southeast for over three hundred li, one reaches Tiemen Pass.
On both sides, the stone cliffs are as dark in color as iron.
The iron gate remains solid and the bells still hang;
this is the western gate of the Han frontier.
Upon exiting the Iron Gate Pass, one arrives [at the next destination].
This is the ancient territory of what was formerly called Tuhuoluo (吐火羅), also known as Tuchuoluo (吐咄羅).
It measures over one thousand *li* from south to north and over three thousand *li* from east to west;
to the east, it borders the Pamir Mountains.
To the west it borders Persia;
to the south lies the Great Snow Mountains;
to the north it occupies the Iron Gates.
The great river Vaksu flows westward through its center,
which is divided into twenty-seven kingdoms;
the monks observe the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) beginning on the sixteenth day of the twelfth month.
This is due to the abundance of warmth and heavy rains.
Following the river northward down to the kingdom of Ṭamī, it measures over six hundred *li* from east to west and over four hundred *li* from south to north.
The royal city is more than twenty li in circuit.
There are over ten monasteries with more than a thousand monks.
There are many stūpas—stūpa being a specific name for ancient towers such as thūpa—and Buddha images of miraculous efficacy.
Proceeding further east, one reaches the kingdom of Chieh-wo-yen-na (Khotan).
It is four hundred *li* from east to west and over five hundred *li* from north to south.
The royal city is more than ten *li* in circuit.
There are few monks in the five monasteries.
Traveling further east, one reaches the kingdom of Fenluoma (Pun-nava),
which is over one hundred li from east to west and over three hundred li from south to north.
The royal city is sixteen or seventeen *li* in circuit;
there are two monasteries with only some one hundred monks.
To the east lies the kingdom of Yushuo Juman.
It is over four hundred li wide and more than one hundred li long.
The royal city is over ten li in circuit.
There are two monasteries, and the monks are not numerous.
To the southwest, bordering the Varku River,
one arrives at the kingdom of Kurughāṇa,
which is over two hundred *li* wide and over three hundred *li* long.
The royal city is over ten *li* away [from the previous site].
There are three monasteries with more than one hundred monks.
Continuing eastward, one reaches the kingdom of Khotan (Kao-sha), which is over three hundred *li* wide and over five hundred *li* long.
The royal city is sixteen or seventeen *li* in circuit.
Traveling further east,
one reaches the kingdom of Khotlo.
It extends for more than a thousand *li* in breadth.
The royal city is over twenty *li* in circumference.
To the east, it borders the Pamir Mountains and reaches the kingdom of Kūrmīta.
It is over two thousand li in breadth and more than two hundred li from east to west,
situated in the midst of the Pamir Mountains (Dacongling).
The royal city is over twenty li in circumference.
To the southwest it borders the country of the Oxus River;
to the south it adjoins the country of Śrīkṣetra.
Crossing this river to the south, one reaches the countries of Dharmasthiti and others.
This is as cited in the aforementioned Middle Path [section].
Furthermore, proceeding slightly eastward from the southern gate of the Iron City for over five hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Bāhīka.
Traveling southwest from Daojiu-mi for over five hundred *li*, one reaches the country of Vāgalāṅga.
It is over fifty *li* wide and more than two hundred *li* long;
its capital city is over ten *li* in circuit.
Traveling further south, one reaches the country of Helu-ximinjian, which is over one thousand li in circuit.
Its capital city is approximately fifteen li in circuit.
Continuing northwest, one arrives at the country of Hulu, which is over eight hundred li in circuit.
The capital city is over fifteen li in circuit.
There are more than ten monasteries with five hundred monks.
Traveling further west, one reaches the country of Bāhīka, which is over eight hundred [li] in width.
It is more than four hundred *li* from [the capital].
To the north, it borders the Vāgvatī River. The royal city is over twenty *li* in circuit;
because its customs are excellent, the people of the country call it the "Little Rājagṛha."
The monastery has more than one hundred monks and over two thousand people,
all of whom study the Hīnayāna.
To the southwest outside the city lies the Navasa (translated here as "New") Monastery, situated to the north of the Snow Mountains.
The various masters who composed the treatises praised and honored this monastery, ensuring its foundations and legacy remained unshaken.
Its images were adorned with rare jewels, and a statue of Vaiśravaṇa stood as its guardian.
When the Turkic Yehe wished to raid the monastery to seize its treasures, [the deity] protected it.
While his army was stationed beside the temple, he dreamed at night that the Heavenly King’s long halberd pierced his chest;
the Khan suffered heart pain and died as a result.
Inside the hall was a Buddha’s bathing pitcher with a capacity of more than one sheng.
Its variegated colors dazzle the eyes, such that even metal or stone cannot easily describe it.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha’s tooth, over one cun in length and eight or nine fen in width;
its color is yellowish-white, and it is radiant and pure.
The Buddha’s broom was made of *kāśa* grass;
it was over two feet long and about seven inches in circumference,
with a handle adorned with various jewels.
On the day of the Three-Substance Fast,
both monastics and laypeople perceived a great radiance being emitted;
there was a large stupa over two hundred feet high.
It was plastered with diamond mud and adorned with jewels;
whenever there were relics of the Buddha, they emitted divine light.
Furthermore, for all the Arhats who had entered nirvana, stupas were erected to manifest their spiritual powers.
Although there were those who had realized the fruits of the path, they did not erect monuments for those who did not manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
To the northwest of the royal city, at a distance of more than fifty *li*, is the city of Trapuṣa; to the north of the royal city, at a distance of more than forty *li*, is the city of Bhallika.
Each has a stupa approximately thirty feet high,
which was erected by the elder who offered parched grain and hair and nails to Śākyamuni during his *kāśyapa* era.
[The relics include] a *saṃghāṭī*, an *uttarāsaṅga*, and a *saṃkakṣikā*.
Furthermore, he inverted his alms bowl and stood his mendicant’s staff upright, arranging them in succession.
He established a stupa according to the ritual, commanding that it be constructed seventy *li* west of the royal city.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, a stupa was built there, standing over twenty feet high.
Furthermore, traveling southwest from the great city for over thirty *li* along the Snow Mountains River,
one arrives at the country of Raivata, which is five or six hundred *li* wide and over one hundred *li* long.
The royal city is over ten li in circuit.
Traveling further southwest for three hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Hu-shih-jian.
It is over five hundred li wide and more than a thousand li long; the royal city is over twenty li in circuit and abounds in mountains and rivers.
Proceeding further northwest, one arrives at the country of Tala-kāṇa.
Its extent is the same as previously mentioned, being over fifty *li* wide.
The royal city is more than ten *li* in circumference, and to its west it borders on the kingdom of Persia.
Furthermore, traveling east from the country of Bāhīka, one reaches the country of Hu-li-ni.
From there, proceeding southeast for more than a thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Ho-lu-si-min-chien.
To the north of this, near the country of Po-kia-lang, is [the aforementioned location].
It is over fifty *li* from east to west.
To the northeast of this country borders the kingdom of Huo.
Furthermore, traveling more than one hundred *li* south from the kingdom of Bāhīka, one reaches the kingdom of Jie-zhi, which is over five hundred *li* wide and over three hundred *li* long.
The capital city is approximately five li in circuit.
There are more than ten monasteries with over three hundred monks,
all of whom study the Hīnayāna.
The mountain ridges connect and extend southeast into the Great Snow Mountains for over six hundred li,
emerging from the ancient territory of Tukhāra;
one then arrives at the kingdom of Bāmiyān.
It is over two thousand *li* wide and more than three hundred *li* long.
Situated amidst the Snow Mountains, its city relies on the perilousness of the cliffs.
There are several tens of monasteries with several thousand monks.
They study the Lokottaravāda school of the Hīnayāna.
To the northeast of the royal city, on a mountain slope,
there is a stone Buddha statue one hundred and fifty feet high.
It is adorned with gold and jewels.
Furthermore, to the left of the Eastern Temple, there is a standing image of Śākyamuni made of brass,
over one hundred feet in height.
The statue was cast in separate sections and assembled;
it stands three *li* east of the city.
The temple contains a plain (unadorned) reclining Buddha in the posture of *nirvāṇa*.
It is over a thousand *chi* in length and is likewise adorned with gold and jewels.
More than two hundred *li* to the southeast, crossing the Great Snow Mountains to the east,
there is a monastery containing a tooth of the Buddha and a tooth of a Pratyekabuddha from the beginning of the eon (*kalpa*).
It is over five inches long and slightly less than four inches wide.
There is also a tooth of a Golden Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), three inches long and two inches wide.
Furthermore, there is the iron alms bowl of Śāṇakavāsa—that is, Śāṇakavāsa, the third patriarch of the Dharma transmission and a Great Arhat.
It measured nine *śronas* in capacity;
it was a nine-panel *saṃghāṭī* robe of deep crimson color,
woven from the fibers of *śaṇa* grass.
Because in a previous life during the summer retreat,
he had offered this grass to the Saṃgha; through the power of that merit,
five hundred beings in the intermediate state (antarābhava) were born and have been wearing it constantly.
Emerging together with the fetus, it grows along with the body;
at the time of the *anujñā* ceremony, it transforms into Dharma robes,
and after the full ordination (*upasampadā*), it further transforms into the nine-striped robe.
His tooth, alms bowl, and other relics were all encased in gold.
By the power of his wisdom and vows, the Arhat entered the samādhi of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*) and remained in his *kāṣāya* robes until the end of the Dharma.
Only then did it undergo transformation and decay; that it has now been somewhat diminished is indeed a sign of its reality.
To the east of the Great Snowy Mountains lies a small river marsh, which flows eastward into the Snowy Mountains.
Crossing the Black Ridge, one arrives at the kingdom of Kāpiśī.
It is over four thousand *li* in circuit;
it has the Snow Mountains to its north and borders the Black Ridge on three sides.
The capital city is more than ten li in circuit.
There are over one hundred monasteries with more than six thousand monks.
Many study the Mahāyāna.
The king believes in the Buddha and annually casts a silver image eighteen feet tall, which he personally maintains and makes offerings to.
There are several dozen deva temples with over a thousand followers of heterodox paths. Three li to the northeast of the royal city, there is [a site].
At the foot of the mountain is a great temple with a Buddha hall.
At the southern side of the eastern gate is a statue of the Great Devarāja;
beneath his right foot lies a great treasure trove.
Recently, a neighboring king pursued the monks with the intent to excavate [the site].
A divine image of a parrot within a crown flapped its wings and cried out, causing the earth to tremble.
The king’s army all collapsed; they rose and apologized, then returned home.
On the ridge to the north of the temple, there are several stone chambers,
which also contain much treasure. Should anyone wish to open them for private gain, [they will encounter obstacles].
Yakṣas transformed themselves into lions, snakes, and insects,
coming to cause a violent upheaval.
Three *li* to the west of the chamber, atop a great mountain ridge, there is an image of Avalokiteśvara.
The image of the Honored One of Sincere Vows manifests a wondrous body to bring peace to those who practice according to their words.
It is located more than thirty li to the southeast of the city.
The Hlu-lo-hu-lo Monastery was constructed by a high minister and named after him;
its stupa is over one hundred feet in height.
Formerly, while I was dreaming at night, I was commanded to construct a stupa and requested śarīra from the King.
When morning came, I arrived at the palace.
There was a person holding a stupa containing śarīra;
the minister detained the śarīra and ordered others to enter first.
He then ascended the stupa with the vessel, and when he overturned the bowl, it opened of its own accord.
Once the śarīra had been securely enshrined,
the king sent messengers to retrieve them, but the stone had already closed.
On the day of the fast, it emitted light and flowed with black oil.
At night, one hears the sound of music.
More than two hundred li to the northwest of the city,
at the summit of the Great Snow Mountains, there is a dragon lake.
At the foot of the mountain, a temple was established for the Dragon.
Within its stupa were over one sheng of the Buddha’s bone and flesh śarīras;
at times, smoke would rise, or sometimes there would be fierce flames like fire.
When the gradual extinguishing was complete, the śarīra were revealed;
they resembled white pearls that circled a pillar, entered the clouds, and returned to descend into the stūpa. To the northwest of the city, on the southern bank of the great river.

In the temple of King Kō (Gukwangsa), there are the infant teeth of the Buddha from his youth, measuring over one cun in length. Furthermore, to the southeast of this [temple], at the temple of King Kō, there is a single fragment of the Buddha’s cranial bone.
It is over an inch wide and yellowish-white in color;
the hair follicles are distinct, and the Buddha’s hair is blue-black,
curling to the right in spirals.
The strips of paper are over a foot long and about an inch wide when rolled up.
Furthermore, to the southwest is the Ancient Queen Consort Temple,
where there is a gilded copper pagoda over one hundred feet high.
The Buddha’s relics, amounting to more than one *sheng*,
emit light every night of the fifteenth day, circling the reliquary dish until dawn when they enter the stūpa.
To the southwest of the city is Mount Bīlaparvata, also known as Gajapṛṣṭha (Elephant Back).
A stupa over one hundred feet high was erected upon a flat rock;
it contains more than one *śera* of relics.
On a cliff to the north of the mountain is a spring where the Buddha, having accepted a meal from a mountain deity, partook of food.
He rinsed his mouth and chewed on a willow branch;
because of this, it grew into a lush grove today,
and the temple was named "Willow Branch" (Yangzhi).
Furthermore, traveling eastward from the Dragon Lake for more than six hundred *li*,
he crossed the Snow Mountains and traversed the Black Ridge to reach the borders of Northern India.
All the districts prior to this were collectively known as the Hu Kingdom;
it is only upon reaching this place that one arrives at the Middle Way.
The name of this land is the Kingdom of Lanpo, which is included within North India.
Entering the territory of the Brahmins of India: the realm of the five Indias is over ninety thousand li in circumference;
it borders the great ocean on three sides and has the Snow Mountains as its northern back.
It is broad in the north and narrow in the south, shaped like a half-moon.
More than seventy kingdoms share the same royal command. As for the kingdom of Lanpā, it lies to the west of Lake Anavatapta.
It borders the Kingdom of Huohuo to the north;
its three southeastern frontiers are bordered by the Black Range.
To the north lies the Snow Mountains. The capital city is approximately ten li in circuit.
There are more than ten monasteries with a small number of monks,
most of whom study the Mahāyāna.
There are several dozen deva temples, where followers of heterodox paths are particularly numerous.

Traveling southeast for more than one hundred *li*, crossing a great mountain range and a large river, one arrives at the kingdom of Nāgarahāra, which belongs to North India. This is the ancient city of Puṣpapura (the City of Flowers), measuring over six hundred *li* in breadth and over two hundred *li* in length.
Mountains surround its four borders, and the capital city is over twenty li in circuit.
There are many monasteries but few monks.
There are five deva temples.
There are one hundred followers of heterodox paths.
Two li to the east of the city is a stone stupa three hundred feet high;
its stone slabs rise up in tiers, and its carvings and engravings are extraordinary.
This is precisely the place where, in a former time, he encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara;
it is the spot where he spread his deerskin garment and hair-cloth upon the muddy ground,
which remains preserved even after the passing of kalpas.
King Aśoka, out of reverence for the Dharma, erected this stone stupa to commemorate it;
on every fast day, the heavens would shower down rain, which the assembled multitude would come to observe.
To the west is a Buddhist monastery, and further south is a small stupa.
This is the place where the mud was concealed;
the King avoided the main road and established it in a secluded spot.
Within the city, the old foundations of a great stūpa already existed.
The separate stupa for the Buddha’s tooth is over three zhang in height;
it is said to have come from the sky, and as it was not made by human hands,
it truly possesses many miraculous wonders.
More than ten li to the southwest of the city is a stūpa, which marks the place where the Buddha descended from the air while traveling from Central India.

To the east of that is another stūpa, marking the place where he formerly purchased flowers upon meeting Dīpaṃkara Buddha. More than twenty li to the southeast of the city, atop a small rocky ridge, stands a stūpa over two hundred feet high.
To the southwest, there is a deep ravine with waterfalls cascading over precipitous cliffs.
On the eastern bank, within a great cave in the rocky wall, dwells the Dragon King;
its entrance is narrow and dark.
In the past, the Buddha manifested here to convert a dragon and left behind a shadow-image that is as radiant as his true form;
to those who pray with utmost sincerity, it briefly appears clearly.
On the square stone outside the cave, there are Buddha footprints marked with the *cakra* (wheel) sign, from which light emanates.
At the northwest corner of the cave is a stūpa at the place where the Buddha walked;
adjacent to it is another stūpa for his hair and nail relics.
Furthermore, it is said that on a large flat rock to the west of the Agnidatta Cave,
there is the impression of a monastic robe having been washed upon it.
More than thirty li to the southeast of the city is the city of Hīla.
Its perimeter is secure and fortified, and within it stands a multi-storied pavilion upon which the Buddha’s cranial bone is enshrined.
It is two inches by Zhou measure and yellowish-white in color.
If one wishes to know whether [the marks] are auspicious or inauspicious, they will appear according to one's intention when impressed with fragrant clay; the hair-pores are clearly distinct.
There is a Buddha’s skull shaped like a lotus leaf,
its color identical to that of a cranial bone.
There is a Buddha’s eye, as large as a jujube fruit.
Pure and translucent,
these were all placed within small stupas made of the seven precious gems to enshrine the aforementioned three traces;
these were further contained within jeweled caskets and sealed shut.
There was the Buddha’s great robe, made of fine cotton wool and yellow in color, placed within a precious casket;
it showed slight signs of deterioration.
Inside [the casket] was the Buddha’s mendicant staff, with rings made of white iron and a shaft made of sandalwood.
It was contained within a precious casket.
A courtier, relying on his power, attempted to bring it into the palace, but it immediately returned to its original place; these are the five sacred traces.
The King ordered five pure practitioners (*pañca-śīlavat*) to attend to and protect it;
those who wished to see it were required to pay a tax of one gold coin.

It is requested that the five categories of precious items be taxed, so that the offerings and veneration may become even more frequent. To the northwest of the pavilion is a small stupa, which is highly efficacious.
When people touched its surface with their hands, the bells would vibrate.
From there, traveling southeast through mountain valleys for over five hundred *li*, one reaches the country of Gandhāra in North India; it is over one thousand *li* wide and eight hundred *li* long.
To the east it borders the Xindu River.
The capital city is over forty li in circuit;
there are few inhabited areas, with only about ten monasteries remaining.

There are one hundred deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together. To the northeast of the city, the old foundations of the precious terrace for the Buddha’s almsbowl remain; it has stood there for several hundred years.
It is now being venerated within the palace of the King of Persia.
Eight or nine *li* to the southeast of the city is a *pippala* tree,
over one hundred feet high, its branches and leaves dense and thick.
Beneath where the four Buddhas of the past sat, there are images seen seated.
The tradition states that all the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa have sat beneath it.
In the past, after Śākyamuni Tathāgata had sat here, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
Later, King Kaniṣka gathered my bones and flesh here.
The king subsequently built a stūpa base to the south, one li and a half in circumference,
with a twenty-five-tiered gilded copper *cakra* pinnacle.
Some say that the forty-tiered structure stands five hundred and fifty feet high and contains one *hu* of śarīra.
Initially, there was a transformed cowherd who constructed a small stūpa three feet high among the trees;
the king threw it away.
Then, at the base of the second tier of the great stupa,
a small stupa appeared halfway out from the side of the stone foundation;
those who were ill were swiftly healed.
On the stone steps on the eastern side of that great stūpa,
there once were golden ants as large as fingers or barley grains,
which followed one another in biting the stone wall until the patterns appeared like carvings.
In the latrine, he fashioned two seated Buddha images out of gold dust,
four, five, and six feet in height respectively.
