Furthermore, on the stone steps facing south, he [placed them].
They painted an image of the Buddha sixteen feet tall.
Long ago, there were two poor men who each offered one gold coin to jointly paint a single image.
"Please manifest a supernatural transformation.
Immediately, the image appeared from the chest upward,
dividing itself into two bodies.
The lower [part] merges into one.
Next, more than a hundred paces to the south, there is a white stone Buddha image sixteen feet high, facing north;
it emits light that appears at night and circles the stupa.
When bandits wished to steal the image, it went out to meet them;
when the bandits retreated, the image returned.
To the left and right of the great stupa are several hundred small stupas.
The craftsmanship of this stupa is exceedingly skillful, and its fragrance and sound are both extraordinary;
sages and immortals circumambulate it,
for the Buddha has prophesied that this is a great stupa.
The Buddha-dharma will only perish after being burned seven times and rebuilt seven times;
it has already been burned three times, and now the construction is currently underway.
To the west are old temples, all of which were established by former kings.
The location where the great masters, such as the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu and the master Pārśva— who was like a wish-fulfilling tree—
composed the *Vibhāṣā*.
Traveling more than fifty *li* northeast from the monastery,
one crosses a great river and arrives at the city of Puṣkarāvatī,
which is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit.
To the east are four stūpas where the Buddhas preached the Dharma, built by King Aśoka;

they are several hundred feet high and their carvings and engravings are rarely seen in this world. Five li to the north of the city, to the east of the old temple, is a stūpa several hundred feet high.
This is the place where the Bodhisattva abandoned his thousand eyes.
To the east, there is a stone stupa over one hundred feet high,
which was originally adorned with exquisite jewels by Brahmā and Śakra.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the precious [stūpa] changed from gold to stone. Furthermore, traveling northwest for more than fifty li, there is a stūpa where the Buddha converted Hārītī.
Again, traveling north for more than fifty li, there is a stūpa.
This is the place where the Bodhisattva Śaṅkha— here called Xiǎn— was struck by the king’s arrow. Furthermore,
approximately two hundred li to the southeast,
twenty-odd li to the northeast of the city of Mālava, [is the site].
Dantaloka is the same as Mount Dandaka;
the stupa atop its peak is the dwelling place of Sudāna (translated as "Good Tusk"),
where a Brahmin once beat a man and a woman.
Blood flowed and smeared the ground;
now all the grasses and trees are the same crimson color.
Between the crags is a stone chamber where the consort practiced meditative concentration. Again, traveling northwest for more than a hundred *li*.
From the small mountains to the great mountains,
there is a temple and stupa to the south where the monks study the Mahāyāna.
In the past, this was the place where the Great Seer Ekaśṛṅga was corrupted by his daughter.
Fifty *li* northeast of the city of Sha, on a great mountain,
there is a large temple of Mahādeva.
Traveling one hundred and fifty *li* southeast from the shrine,
one arrives at the city of Udakhaṇḍa.
It is more than twenty *li* in circuit.
It borders the Sindhu River to the south.
From this city, traveling six hundred li over the mountains to the north,
one reaches the country of Uddiyāna, which is a principal kingdom of North India.
Ancient records state that the valleys and mountains of Oḍḍiyāna are interconnected and extend for five thousand li;
it was formerly the garden of a Cakravartin king.
The soil is well-suited for saffron.
It is situated between the Suvāstu and the Śatadru rivers.
The royal city is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit.
There is one thousand four hundred monasteries with eighteen thousand monks.
They also study the Mahāyāna;
however, nowadays the practice of the Mahāyāna is mostly neglected and its followers are few.
As for the textual systems, the Vinaya rules, and the transmitted teachings, there are five schools.
1. The Dharmaguptaka school;
2. The Mahīśāsaka school;
3. The Kāśyapīya school.
There are four schools of the Sarvāstivāda and five of the Mahāsāṃghika.
More than ten heterodox temples are interspersed where various sects dwell together. The royal capital is the city of Mathurā.
Five li to the east is the Great Tāra Stūpa;
this is the place where the Buddha, in a former life as the Rishi Kṣāntivādin, was dismembered by Kali—here translated as King Strife.
It is located two hundred and sixty li northeast of the city.
Entering the great mountain, one reaches the spring of the Āpāla Dragon;
this is the very source of the river.
Its tributaries flow to the southwest, freezing in the spring and summer, with snow flying morning and night. It was here that the Buddha formerly converted a violent dragon.
Vajrapāṇi struck the cliff with his vajra;
the nāgas, terrified, took refuge in the Buddha and requested that he release rain, which he then granted.
They order the people to gather grain.
Every twelve years, there is a rain disaster.
Furthermore, more than thirty li to the southwest of the spring...
On a large rock on the northern bank of the river, after the Buddha had subdued the dragon, he left a footprint for him to see;
its length varies according to one's intention.
It extends downstream for more than thirty li.
There is a stone where a Buddha washed his robes, the patterns of the *kāṣāya* appearing as if carved.
Over four hundred li south of the city,
one follows the river upstream through the valleys of the Hiraṇyavatī.
Ascending eastward along the cliffs of flowers and fruits,
one may hear the sounds of clamorous conversation and music;
the square stones join one another.
This is the place where the Buddha formerly gave up his body upon hearing half a verse.

Over two hundred li south of the city, by the side of a great mountain, stands the Mahāvana Monastery (translated as "Great Forest"). Formerly, when the Buddha was King Śraddhala—that is, Sarvadarśa, the "All-Giver"—he lost his kingdom and fled to this region, living as a poor man.
Therefore, he was bound and sent to that place.
More than forty *li* down the mountain to the northwest of the monastery,
there is a temple and a stupa over one hundred feet high.
On a rock to the side, the marks of the Buddha’s footprints emit light that illuminates the monastery.
For the sake of the devas, he preached here concerning his former birthplace. Beneath the stupa is a stone, yellowish-white and oily;
this is the place where the Buddha, in a former life, broke his own bones to transcribe a sutra for the sake of hearing the Dharma. Furthermore, seventy *li* to the west is a stupa.
This is the place where the Buddha, in a former life as King Śibi (here translated as Yú), cut his own flesh to substitute for a dove.

Furthermore, more than two hundred li to the west, along the Sannirāja River at the site of Sarpakṣaya (meaning "snake-destroying" or "antidote to snakes"), there is a temple and stupa eighty feet high.
In the past, when the Buddha was in the body of Śakra, he transformed himself into a great dead python and gave it as alms to a place afflicted by poverty and pestilence;
beside this spot is the Soma Stūpa.
This refers to the matter of the Buddha transforming himself into a *soma* snake to cure those who had eaten it;
at the cliff-tower to the north of the valley, many were healed through seeking [the Buddha] there.
Furthermore, there is a spring that gushes forth nearby.
In the past, the Buddha was a peacock king;
he used his beak to peck out [a thorn] to save those afflicted by illness. It is located seventy li southwest of the city, east of a great river.
The stupa is sixty feet high.
This was built by King Uttarasena, also known as Shangjun (Upper Army).
The Buddha commanded that his relics be divided and given to the king, who erected a stūpa on the riverbank.
The king carried them back on a white elephant, which transformed into stone.
More than fifty *li* west of the city, one crosses a great river.
There is the Lohityaka Stūpa—meaning "Red"—which is over fifty feet high.
In the past, the Buddha was King Maitrībala.
The Place Where Five Yakṣas Pierced Their Blood for Him:

Thirty *li* to the northeast of the city, there is a stone stūpa forty feet high, where the Buddha preached the Dharma for humans and devas; it is called *Abhuta* (the Extraordinary) in the language of the A-bu-tuo.

The stupa emerged from the earth and remains there to this day. Furthermore, crossing the great river to the west for forty *li*, there is a temple and vihāra containing an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara—*Avalokiteśvara* being translated as "Observer" (*Guān*) and *Īśvara* as "Sovereign" (*Zìzài*). This image, which manifests spiritual responses and radiates its light afar, resides on a mountain ridge one hundred and fifty *li* to the west of here.
The Dragon Pond is more than thirty li in circumference.
To the northeast of the royal city, one crosses the mountain valleys and ascends upstream along the Sindhu River.
The road was extremely perilous;
traveling by means of ropes, plank bridges, and lashed logs, and treading upon stairways,
they reached the Darel River valley after more than a thousand li.
Udyāna was its former capital.
Within a great monastery there is a carved wooden image of the Bodhisattva Maitreya—formerly called Meṭṭiya, and in the language of Tang, Cishi (the Benevolent One).
It was golden and radiant, standing over one hundred feet high.
It was constructed by Madhyāntika— the Arhat Madhyandina— who,
through his supernormal powers, led the artisans up to Tuṣita Heaven (the "Joyous" Heaven).
After three cycles of observing the characteristics, its excellence was perfected;
it was from the time this Image-Dharma first appeared that it began to flow eastward.
Traveling east, it crossed mountain ridges, and against the current, it traversed rivers.
Traveling over dangerous terrain across more than five hundred *li* of flying bridges, he crossed the river;
proceeding further east, he crossed the Bārhū River and, ascending a perilous height,
arrived at the kingdom of Pulo.
It is four thousand *li* in circumference within the Great Snow Mountains;
there are several hundred monasteries stretching from east to west,
with several thousand monks.
The teachers there have many laxities in their observance of the precepts.
That country is not under the jurisdiction of India.
It is frequently covered in ice and snow, and its soil produces gold that is the color of fire.
To the north, it faces the great mountain of Vārāśikhara;
returning from the kingdom of Gandhāra,
it lies south of the city of Udakānanda.
The river Du-xin flows across the river;
it is approximately four li wide and flows toward the southwest, as clear and limpid as a mirror.
Poisonous dragons and fierce beasts dwell within its caves.
Vessels carrying the precious flowers of the śarīra often sink.
Crossing the river, one arrives at the country of Takṣaśilā in North India, which is over two thousand li in circuit.
The capital city is over ten li in circuit.
There are many monasteries but few monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna.
Over seventy li to the northwest of the city, there is [a place].
There is the Ilāvatī Dragon Pond,
measuring more than a hundred paces in circumference.
Thirty li to the southeast of the pond is [the following].
Between the two mountains stands a stupa over one hundred feet high.
The Buddha formerly prophesied that when Maitreya appears in the world,
one of the four great treasuries shall emerge from this place.
Thus there was trembling;
yet within a hundred paces around, not a single person shook.
Those who wished to rise were struck down by the earth's quaking.
Twelve li north of the city is a stupa that regularly emits divine light during the days of fasting.
Celestial flowers fall and heavenly music resounds.
Recently, there was a man afflicted with leprosy who approached it.
At the stupa, he performed prostrations and repentance to purify his defilements and applied fragrant ointments;
before long, his body was healed and became fragrant and clean.
This was at the place where, in the past, the Buddha, for King Candraprabha (also known as Moonlight), offered his head as a gift.
The stupa where he performed his thousandth act of giving is named Candraprabha (Moonlight). To the southeast of the city, on a mountain, there is a stupa approximately ten *zhang* high;
it was built by King Aśoka at the site where King Kṣemadarsin (Decidemujwang) ruled.
Proceeding again southeast for over seven hundred li through mountains and valleys,
one reaches the country of Saṃkāśya, which belongs to North India; it is three thousand five hundred li in circuit.
It borders the Xindu River to the west.
The great city is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit.
Fifty *li* to the east of the city...
There is a stone stupa over twenty zhang high at the site where the Buddha once traveled;
there are more than ten ponds,
their surfaces entirely covered with lotus flowers of four colors.
From here, returning south, he reached the northern border of the kingdom of Takṣaśilā.
Crossing the Indus River, he traveled eastward for more than two hundred li and passed through a great stone gate.
This is the place where the Prince Mahāsattva sacrificed his body to feed a tiger.
To the east is a monastery with over a hundred monks.
Furthermore, one hundred and fifty *li* to the south is a stone stūpa.
The place where the Bodhisattva pierced himself with a bamboo splinter to provide blood for the beast,
as well as the ground and the vegetation there, remain vermilion in color even today.
To the north of this is a stone stūpa over twenty zhang in height.
The emission of light opened their faith, and those suffering from illness were mostly cured.
Furthermore, over fifty li to the east,
there is a temple and stupa on an isolated mountain, more than two hundred feet in height.
The monastic community consists of two hundred people, all of whom study the Mahāyāna.
This is the place where the Buddha formerly converted a yakṣa so that he would no longer eat meat.
Furthermore, traveling over five hundred li southeast from here along the mountains, one reaches [the next destination].
Arrival at the country of Uraśā. It is in Northern India and is over two thousand li in circuit.
Mountains and hills are joined together in succession.
The capital city is eighteen *li* in circuit.
Its inhabitants do not believe in the Buddha-dharma. It belongs to Kaśmīra.
There is a Buddhist stupa over twenty zhang high,
built by King Aśoka.
There is also a monastery where the monks study the Mahāyāna teachings.
Furthermore, traveling southeast by mountain iron bridge for over a thousand *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Kaśmīra, which is in North India.
In ancient times it was called Jibin; it is seven thousand *li* in circuit and is surrounded on all four sides by mountains.
Although the passageways are narrow and inferior, they provide access.
To the west of the city, it borders a great river,
thirteen *li* in length and approximately four *li* in width.
There are over one hundred monasteries with more than five thousand monks.
The soil produces dragon-breed horses, saffron (uraga-keśara), and fire-jewels.
There are four stupas, each containing a little over one *sheng* of śarīra.
In the fourth century after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
the Venerable Pārśva, who was eighty years old when he finally left the household life, attained the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
He brought five hundred arhats to this place to compose one hundred thousand verses.
The *Upadeśa-śāstra* is another name for the *Sūtra-piṭaka*.
Next, he composed the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* in one hundred thousand stanzas.
Next, he composed the *Abhidharma-śāstra* in one hundred thousand stanzas,
totaling six million six hundred thousand words,
which provides a comprehensive exposition of the Tripiṭaka.
More than ten li southeast of the new city, on the northern side of the old city, is the Great Mountain Yangsi Monastery.
There are three hundred monks there, and a Buddha’s tooth, one and a half inches long,
yellowish-white in color, which emits light on fast days.
Furthermore, fifteen li to the south, there is a standing image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Those who wish to see him may do so by fasting.
More than two hundred li to the northwest of the royal city, one reaches the Śāla Forest Monastery.
One hundred and fifty *li* west of the city, where the Great River meets the mountains,
there is a monastery with more than one hundred monks.
From here, traveling southwest across the mountains for over seven hundred *li*, one arrives [at the destination].
The kingdom of Pañcāla is in North India and belongs to the territory of Kaśmīra; it is over two thousand *li* in circuit and contains five monasteries. It is abounding in mountains and rivers.

Traveling southeast for over four hundred *li*, one reaches the kingdom of Aruṇākapura. This is not part of proper North India, but rather a frontier (barbarian) state; it is over four thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city is over one thousand li in circuit.
There are ten monasteries, but the monks are very few.
There is one deva temple, and the non-Buddhists are extremely numerous.
From Lampaṭa, this region is of inferior form and character;
it is not the true land of India.
From here, one descends the mountain and travels southeast.
Furthermore, these are great rivers that flow far away without bound;
they are distinguished only by the river-states that demarcate their regions.
Even the small mountains here all stand as isolated peaks.
From here to the north, it connects with the Snow Mountains;
to the east, it reaches the various snow mountains south of the "Cool Region" (Liangbu) of the Divine Land (Jambudvīpa).
According to this, this mountain is also a great stronghold of Jambudvīpa.
From the southeast of this city, descending to the level plains and crossing a river,
one travels over seven hundred li to reach [it].
The kingdom of Takka is located in North India and is over ten thousand *li* in circuit.
To the east it borders the Vipāśā River,
and to the west it abuts the Sindhu River.
The capital city is over twenty li in circuit.
The local customs have little faith in Buddhism and mostly worship heavenly deities;
there are more than ten Buddhist temples and several hundred deva shrines.
Fifteen li to the southwest of the city is the old city of Śākala.
Its temple and stūpa are over twenty *zhang* high.
This was the place where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma and performed their walking meditations.
Furthermore, about six *li* to the northwest, there is a stūpa over twenty *zhang* high;
this was also a place where four Buddhas preached the Dharma. About ten *li* to the northeast of the New Capital City...
The stone stupa is over twenty zhang high.
It contains many śarīras and emits light on fast days.
Traveling east for more than five hundred li, one arrives at [the next destination].
The country of Na-po-ti (Navatī) is in Northern India and is over two thousand li in circuit.
Its capital city is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit.
There are ten monasteries and eight deva temples.
More than five hundred li to the southeast of the city,
one reaches the Jālīnārāma Monastery, which is over twenty li in circumference.
There are several hundred thousand stupas containing the Buddha’s relics.
There are also stone chambers and other such structures.
The monastic community consists of three hundred people,
who study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna.
His virtuous conduct was pure and lofty, and his knowledge of the minor sciences was extensive.
The thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa all preached the Dharma in this manner.
Three hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni, [this occurred].
Kātyāyana (also known as Kātyāyana) also composed the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* here.
The temple and stupa are over twenty zhang in height.
There are sites where the traces of the walking and sitting of the four Buddhas are preserved.
From here, traveling east for one hundred and fifty *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Śrīnagarī in North India.
It is over one thousand *li* from east to west and six hundred *li* from south to north. The capital city is more than ten *li* in circuit.
There are fifty monasteries with more than two thousand monks, who specialize in various branches of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
There are three deva temples with five hundred non-Buddhists.
Traveling northeast across the mountains for more than seven hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Kuruta in North India. Mountains surround its four borders;
the capital city is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit.
There are more than twenty monasteries with over a thousand monks, most of whom study the Mahāyāna.
There are fifteen deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
[The land] produces fire-pearls and rains down stones.
The common people suffer from goiters and swellings.
Within the city is a stupa marking the place where the Buddha once traveled and preached the Dharma.
From here, traveling north for nearly two thousand li, one arrives at [the next destination].

The mountain roads were perilous as he reached the kingdom of Lohurā in North India. Traveling further north through the mountains for more than two thousand *li*, the snow and cold became even more severe;
he arrived at the kingdom of Maḷava, also known as Sambhaha, which is included within North India. From Kuruta, he traveled southward for more than seven hundred *li*.
Crossing mountains and fording rivers, he arrived at the kingdom of Śatadru, located in North India. It is over two thousand *li* in circuit and borders a great river to the west.
The capital city is seventeen or eighteen *li* in circumference.
The Buddha-dharma flourishes greatly; there are ten monasteries inside and outside the city, and the monks are few in number.
Three *li* to the east of the city is a stūpa over twenty *zhang* high, built by King Aśoka.
Beside it are the walking and sitting traces of four Buddhas.

From here, traveling southwest for more than eight hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, which marks the entry into Central India. It is three thousand *li* in circuit, and its capital city is fifteen *li* in circuit.
There are eight monasteries, and the monks are few in number.
The laity believe in non-Buddhist paths;
there are ten deva temples with more than a thousand followers of heterodox sects.
The soil yields rice that is harvested in sixty days.

Traveling eastward for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Mathurā (in Central India; formerly called Motoulu), which is over five thousand *li* in circuit, with its capital city measuring more than twenty *li*.
There are more than twenty monasteries with over two thousand monks,
who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
There are five deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
There grow in the soil *āmra* fruits;
the small ones are green when unripe and yellow when ripe,
while the large ones remain green from beginning to end.
Within the city are three stupas;
there are many relics of the four Buddhas,
as well as those of Śāriputra.
Maudgalyāyana refers to Maudgalyāyana; Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra refers to Pūrṇa; Upāli refers to Upāli;
Ānanda and Rāhula.
At the various stupas of Mañjuśrī and others,
on each of the three long months, at the six times of day and night,
the monks and nuns assemble as a community for the study of the Abhidharma.
The assembly for making offerings shall pay homage to the stupa of Śāriputra;
the assembly practicing meditative concentration shall pay homage to the stupa of Maudgalyāyana;
and the assembly reciting the sūtras shall pay homage to the stupa of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
The community of monks made offerings at the stupa of Upāli;
the community of nuns made offerings at the stupa of Ānanda;
and the community of those not yet fully ordained made offerings at the stupa of Rāhula.
The Mahāyāna community makes offerings to the stupas of all bodhisattvas;
one should understand that these stupas do not necessarily require the enshrinement of physical remains.
Rather, they are established by fashioning images and providing offerings as an expression of the mind's devotion.
This can be understood by the fact that the noble Mañjuśrī has not yet entered parinirvāṇa.
Six *li* to the east of the city is a mountain cliff monastery;
it was constructed by the venerable Upagupta, also known as Jinhu (Near Protector).
There is a stupa for the Buddha’s fingernails.
To the north of the temple, there is a stone cave chamber twenty feet high and thirty feet wide,
which was filled with four-inch tally sticks.
Regarding the husband and wife who were close protectors and guides and both attained arhatship:
a tally-stick was sent [to mark their number], and those who deviated from this were not recorded in the chamber.
Furthermore, more than twenty li to the southeast of the chamber...
Beside the Great Dried-up Pond there is a stūpa.
Once, when the Buddha was traveling there, a monkey offered him honey.
The Buddha had it mixed with water so that the entire assembly could drink it together.
The monkey, overjoyed, fell into a pit and died;
he was then reborn among human beings in a forest north of the pond, at a place where four Buddhas had practiced walking meditation.
There are many remaining traces [of past sites].

Traveling further northeast for more than five hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Sādhūniṣevana in Central India. It is over seven thousand li in circuit, and its capital city is over twenty li in circuit.
There are three monasteries with seven hundred monks,
all of whom follow the Hinayana.
There are more than a hundred deva temples, and followers of various heterodox paths are very numerous.
Four li to the northwest of the city is a stūpa over twenty zhang high containing one sheng of śarīra, which frequently emits great light.
Over a hundred li to the south of the city, one reaches a Buddhist temple.
Furthermore, more than four hundred li to the northeast, one arrives at [another site].
The country of Suruḷkna is in Central India and is more than six thousand *li* in circuit.

Its eastern border is largely desolate and borders the Gaṅgā River—that is, the ancient Ganges—which flows northward from the great mountains; to the southeast of the capital city lies the Yamunā River.
It flows out from the mountains to the northwest of the kingdom, passing through the central territory.
The capital city is over twenty li in circuit and borders the Yamunā River to the east.
There are five monasteries with more than a thousand monks, most of whom study the Hīnayāna.
There are more than a hundred deva temples, and followers of various heterodox paths are very numerous.
Outside the eastern gate of the Great Monastery in Hexi is a stupa;
it was here that the Buddha once preached the Dharma and delivered sentient beings.
Beside it stands a stūpa containing the Buddha’s hair and nail relics.
Over eight hundred li east of the Yamunā River, one reaches the source of the Gaṅgā,
which is three or four li wide.
Entering the sea to the southeast for more than ten *li*, the water is a deep azure color, sweet in taste, and its fine sands flow along with the current.
According to local custom, this is called "Blessed Water" (*Fushui*); bathing therein removes one's sins.
Some even cast away their lives by drowning themselves,
claiming they would be reborn in heaven to enjoy bliss.
There was the Bodhisattva Deva of the country of Siṃhala.
This is the place where the non-Buddhists were converted and received the True Dharma.
Crossing the river to the east, one arrives at the country of Mathurā. Central India is over six thousand li in circuit, and its capital city is over twenty li in circuit.
They do not believe in the Buddha but revere the gods.
There are more than ten monks in the monastery, with over eight hundred people, most of whom follow the Hīnayāna.
There are more than fifty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
On the eastern bank of the Gaṅgā River, at the northwestern border of the kingdom,
lies the city of Mathurā, which is more than twenty li in circuit.
It produces brass and crystal.
Beside the city it borders a great river.
There is a great temple of Mahādeva that possesses much awe-inspiring power.
There is a pond with stone embankments, where the river is channeled to form a cove.
The five regions of India regard the confluence of the Gaṅgā River as a place for generating merit and extinguishing transgressions;
hundreds of thousands of people constantly bathe there.
Traveling three hundred *li* north from Mathurā, one arrives [at this site].
Upon arrival, [he reached] the country of Brahmapura in North India, which is over four thousand *li* in circuit and surrounded on all four sides by mountains.
The capital city is over twenty *li* in circuit; there are five monasteries with few monks.
In the deva temples, there dwell ten kinds of heterodox practitioners.
To the north of the kingdom, beyond the Great Snow Mountains, lies the country of Suvarṇagotra (in the language of the country, meaning "Gold-clan"), which produces superior gold.
The region extending eastward is the country of Tazig (Dongnüguo),
which is not included within India;
it is also known as the country of Great Yangtong (Dayangtongguo).
To the east it borders on Tibet, to the west on Sambhaha,
and to the north on Khotan;
for generations, this kingdom has been ruled by women as its kings.
Furthermore, the king does not concern himself with state affairs;
the men do nothing but engage in military expeditions and cultivate the fields.
Traveling southeast from the country of Matipura for over four hundred *li*, one arrives [at this place].
In the country of Goviśanā in Central India, the circumference is over two thousand *li*, and the capital city is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit.
There are two monasteries with over one hundred monks who study the Hīnayāna.
There are more than thirty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
The city walls are solid and steep.
Beside them stands an ancient monastery with a stupa over twenty zhang in height.
The Buddha once preached the Dharma here for one month.
There are two stupas containing his hair and nail relics, each over ten feet high,
with the footprints of the four Buddhas nearby.
Traveling southeast again for more than four hundred *li*,
one arrives at the country of Ākṣaśīlā. Central India is over three thousand *li* in circuit,
and its capital city is seventeen or eighteen *li* in circuit.
There are more than ten monasteries with over a thousand monks,
who study the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are nine deva temples with more than three hundred non-Buddhist practitioners.
The city relies on natural fortifications;
by the side of its outer moat is the site where the Buddha preached the Dharma to the nāgas for seven days.
A stūpa has been erected there, beside which are the footprints of the four Buddhas, both walking and sitting.
A stupa was erected to mark this spot.
Furthermore, traveling two hundred and seventy *li* to the south, one crosses the Gaṅgā River.
To the southwest lies the kingdom of Vīraśanā; India is over two thousand *li* in circuit, and its capital city is over ten *li* in circuit.
Those who believe in non-Buddhist paths are few, and they show little respect for the Buddha-dharma.
There are two monasteries with three hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna.
There are five deva temples.
The temples and stupas within the city are over ten *zhang* in height.
It was here that the Buddha once expounded upon the *skandhas* and *dhātus* for seven days.
The traces of the walking and sitting of the four Buddhas still remain in this place.
Traveling east for more than two hundred li,
one arrives at Kāpiśī, an ancient monastic center (saṃghārāma) of Central India, with a circumference of more than two thousand li.
Its capital city has a circumference of more than twenty li.
There are four monasteries with more than a thousand monks.
There are ten deva temples dedicated to Maheśvara;
all of them fashion images of the deity.
Their male organs are extremely long and large in form;
the common people do not consider this to be a fault,
claiming that all sentient beings are born from celestial organs.
More than twenty li to the east of the city, within a great monastery housing several hundred monks,
there reside tens of thousands of lay devotees (upāsakas) by the side of the temple.
Inside the great enclosure wall stands a triple staircase for the Three Jewels, constructed by the Heavenly Emperor.
The middle tier was made of gold;
the left was of crystal,
and the right was of white silver.
Arranged north to south, it faces east on the lower level.
This is the place where the Buddha, having ascended from the Jeta Grove (Śītavana) to the Sudharmā Hall in heaven to preach the Dharma to his mother for three months, descended.
The steps from a hundred years ago still existed;
now they have all vanished.
A later king modeled his own after them.
It is still over seventy feet high.
A vihāra has been erected atop it, and beside it stands a stone pillar, smooth and lustrous, reflecting clearly;
according to one's sins or merits, an image appears within the pillar.
There is a stupa beside the steps built by King Aśoka.
It contains the walking and sitting traces of the four Buddhas.
A stupa was also erected at the place where the Buddha bathed.
There is a Buddha’s chamber within the vihāra,
and beside it is a stone terrace where the Buddha practiced walking meditation,
fifty paces long and seven feet high.
The places trodden by his feet were all marked with lotus patterns.
To the left and right of the base are small stupas built by Brahmā.
Further forward is the place where the nun Padmā, having transformed herself into a universal monarch, first beheld the Buddha.
The Buddha told the nun, "It was not you who came first.
There was Subhūti, son of Sūbhadra, who sat in meditative seclusion within a stone chamber;
he realized the emptiness of all phenomena and beheld my Dharma-body."
Next, to the southeast, there is a pond where a dragon dwells;
it constantly guards the sacred traces and must not be lightly violated.
From here, traveling northwest for two hundred li less [than the previous distance], one arrives.
Kanyakubja is the city of Kanyākubja in Central India; it is over four thousand *li* in circuit. The western part of the capital city is near the Gaṅgā River;
it is more than twenty *li* long and four or five *li* wide.
There are over one hundred monasteries where heterodox and orthodox traditions coexist;
the monastic community numbers more than ten thousand, studying both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
There are also over two hundred deva temples.
There were several thousand followers of other paths.
He was the sovereign king of the five Indias, known as Śīlāditya, which means "Sun of Virtue" (Jièrì). He belonged to the Vaiśya caste.
When he was first about to ascend the throne,
there was an image of Avalokiteśvara on the banks of the Gaṅgā;
he then made a request of it.
He said to him:
"You were originally a bhikṣu in this forest hermitage;
now that King Candrakaṇṇa has extinguished the Buddha-dharma."
"Your Majesty should once again give rise to compassion for all beings and keep them in your heart.
Only then, O King, over the five realms, may you cautiously ascend the lion throne and assume the title of Great King.
Thereupon, the King [conversed] with Prince Kumāra.
He completely exterminated the followers of the heretical Moon King and issued a strict decree stating that anyone who ate meat should have their tongue cut off.
For taking life, one's hand shall be severed.
He then shared governance of the state with his younger sister.
Along the banks of the Ganges, he constructed a thousand stūpas.
Each was over a hundred feet high.
In the cities, towns, villages, thoroughfares, and crossroads,
they erected vihāras and stored provisions.
He ceased the practice of medicine and bestowed his bounty upon the destitute and poor.
At all sites containing sacred traces, he established monasteries.
Every five years for twenty years, a great assembly was convened.
He emptied his treasuries and storehouses to provide relief to all living beings,
retaining only his weapons to prepare for unforeseen emergencies.
On the day the assembly was first convened, he gathered monks from various nations.
For twenty-one days, they provided the four requisites as offerings and had them engage in debate;
[he sought] one whose preceptual conduct was steadfast and firm, and whose virtue and realization were excellent and harmonious.
Having ascended the lion throne, the King received the precepts;
though he was pure and beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), he manifested reverence and veneration toward those whose defiled conduct was exposed.
They were driven out of the kingdom's borders.
As for all those kings and ministers who planted merit without indolence,
they sat together with their hands joined.
Otherwise, they would not be spared.
When the king tours the various regions and customs, he does not reside in one place permanently;
wherever he travels, the fourfold army must lead the way with strict military preparations.
They traveled by boat and on elephants, beating drums and blowing conch shells.
With eighty thousand elephant troops, they intimidated the regions in the four directions; for two or three months, they did not travel beyond the borders.
Within the palace, they provided daily meals for the śramaṇas.
There were one thousand monks and five hundred brahmins;
they divided the day into three periods: one period for attending to administrative affairs and two periods for cultivating merit.
Furthermore, he abstained from eating meat and blood,
taking only one meal per day.
To the east of Hexi Temple, he erected a jeweled terrace over a hundred feet high.
Within it is a golden image of equal size to the Buddha's body.
To the south of this, a jeweled altar has been erected as the place for bathing the Buddha image.
Approximately fifteen *li* to the northeast of here, [is another site].
A separate palace was constructed, leading from the temple to the palace;
pavilions were built along both sides of the road, adorned with every kind of exquisite carving and ornamentation.
The musicians did not move, yet they performed in succession.
Furthermore, a three-foot golden image was set upon a great elephant draped with precious curtains;
the King, acting as the image of Śakra, stood as his left attendant holding a precious parasol.
There was King Kumāra of the country of Kāmboja, also known as "The Youth," who appeared in the likeness of Brahmā, holding a fly-whisk and attending on the right;
each was accompanied by five hundred elephant troops clad in armor, providing joint protection.
There were one hundred great elephants each before and behind [the procession].
Musicians atop them played drums and instruments.
King Śīlāditya, moreover, scattered offerings of pearls, various jewels, gold, silver, and flowers as they emerged, making offerings to the Triple Gem.
In the five regions of India, nuns are rare; even where there are nuns,
they belong to the same monastic lineage as the monks,
eat in the same places, and do not violate their disciplinary precepts.
However, Prince Tóngzǐ was of the Kṣatriya caste;
he spoke to his messenger, Lǐ Yìbiǎo, saying:
"For four thousand years, this has been handed down through successive generations."
In former times, a divine being flew here from the land of Han.
The King [established] his capital in this territory;
to the northwest of the city is a stupa built by King Aśoka.
In the past, the Buddha preached the Dharma here for seven days.
Beside it is a stupa containing his hair and nails,
as well as the walking and sitting traces of the four Buddhas.
Furthermore, it borders the Gaṅgā River to the south;
three monasteries share a single enclosure with separate gates,
and their Buddha statues are magnificent and resplendent.
The Buddha’s tooth is one and a half inches long;
its luster and color have undergone transformation, and it is enshrined within a precious casket.
Those who come from near and far to behold it number in the hundreds and thousands every day.
The guardians were distressed by the heavy taxes on gold and jewels,
yet those who delighted in the ritual did not decline the heavy offerings;
on the day of the fast, they were immediately brought out and placed upon a high seat.
Although flowers were scattered there in abundance, they did not sink into the tooth-relic casket.
The monks of the monastery were pure and disciplined, numbering several thousand households.
To the left and right of the temple stood vihāras over one hundred feet high.
The image within the brick chamber on a stone foundation is adorned with jewels, or perhaps made entirely of gold and silver. Next, to the southeast, is a great vihāra.
It stands upon a stone foundation of brickwork and is over twenty zhang in height.
This is where the Buddha spent six months teaching on the body’s impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and impurity.
Furthermore, there are the walking and sitting traces of four Buddhas,
located six or seven li to the southeast of the city.
On the southern bank of the Gaṅgā River,
more than one hundred li to the southeast of the city,
there is the city of Navadevakula.
It is situated on the eastern bank of the Gaṅgā River;
three monasteries share a single enclosure with separate gates, measuring over twenty li in circumference. It is located some two hundred paces further forward from that point.
The stupa is over twenty zhang in height.
It is the place where the Buddha once preached the Dharma for seven days.
Within it are śarīra relics that occasionally emit radiance.
Beside it are the walking and sitting traces of four Buddhas.
Four li to the north of the monastery, on the bank of the Gaṅgā,
is a stūpa over twenty zhang high, where the Buddha once preached the Dharma for seven days.
Four hundred hungry ghosts attained awakening and were reborn in heaven.
Beside it is a stupa for hair and nail relics;
further beside it are the walking and sitting traces of the four Buddhas.
Traveling again southeast for more than six hundred li, crossing the Ganges River to the south, one arrives at the kingdom of Aśvada.
India is more than five thousand li in circuit, and its capital city is over twenty li in circuit.
The monastery has more than one hundred monks and over three thousand people;
they study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

There are ten deva temples, and the followers of heterodox paths are few. The old temple within the city is where Vasubandhu Bodhisattva—also known as Śeṣin—composed his treatises on both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna for several decades.
Five li north of the city, on the bank of the Gaṅgā,
within a great monastery, there is a stupa over twenty zhang high.
It was here that the Buddha preached the Dharma for three months for the sake of devas and humans.
To the side are Buddhist stupas and the walking and sitting traces of the four Buddhas.
Five li to the west of the monastery is a stupa containing the hair and nail relics of the Buddha.
Five li to the southwest of the city [is another].
In the old monastery within the great Āmrapālī Grove,
the Bodhisattva Asaṅga— also known as Wuzhuo— ascended to the celestial palace at night and received from Maitreya the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,
the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra*, the *Madhyānta-vibhaṅga*, and other such treatises.
Xiao explained this to the assembly.
About one hundred paces northwest of the grove is the stupa containing the Buddha’s hair and nail relics.
From here, traveling east for more than three hundred li:
Crossing to the north of the Gaṅgā,
one arrives at the kingdom of Ayomukha in Central India, which is two thousand five hundred li in circuit.
Its capital borders the river and is twenty li in circuit.
There are five monasteries with over a thousand monks who study the Hīnayāna.
There are ten deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together. To the southeast of the city, bordering the Gaṅgā River, stands a stūpa more than twenty *zhang* in height.
This is the place where the Buddha once preached the Dharma for three months.
There is a blue stone stūpa containing his hair and nail relics,
and the walking and sitting traces of the four Buddhas.
Traveling southeast again for more than seven hundred *li*, one crosses the Gaṅgā River and reaches the northern bank of the Yamunā River in the kingdom of Prayāga.
India is over five thousand *li* in circuit, and its capital city is situated at the confluence of two rivers.
The city is more than twenty *li* in circuit; there are two monasteries with few monks, while there are several hundred deva temples, so that followers of heterodox paths are particularly numerous.
To the southwest of the city, it borders the bend of the Yamunā River for two or three thousand *li*.
Between the confluence of the northeast-flowing rivers, there are *campaka* flowers.
In the forest stands a stupa over ten zhang high,
the site where the Buddha once subdued the non-Buddhists.
There are hair-and-nail stupas and the sites of his walking meditations.
Furthermore, there is the place where the Bodhisattva Deva composed the *Śataśāstra-vṛtti*. In front of the celestial temple within the city, there is a large tree with dense and luxuriant foliage.
Man-eating demons rely upon it;
the remains of those left behind form a pyre.
When people reach the shrine, there is none who does not treat their own lives with contempt.
Having climbed a tree and thrown himself down, he was enticed by a ghost. Between the two rivers to the east of the city, the area extends for more than ten *li* in length and breadth;
the terrain is level and high, with fine sand spread across it.
From ancient times to the present, kings, nobles, and others who have made offerings have never failed to stop here.
It is known as the Great Field of Almsgiving.
King Śīlāditya also practiced this work there.
At the confluence of rivers to the east of the field, it is located.
Every day, several hundred people drown themselves to death there;
according to local custom, this place is called the "Abode of Those Reborn in Heaven.
Those who wish to practice the Dharma remain without food for seven days at this site.
They submerged themselves in the middle of the stream, with people from near and far rushing toward them;
even mountain apes and wild deer wandered in groups along the water's edge, abandoning their food to plunge into the water.
When King Śīlāditya was practicing the giving of alms,
two macaques were present; the female was killed by a dog,
and the male carried her corpse and threw it into this river.
He again starved himself for several days until he died. From there,
traveling southwest through a great forest wilderness for over five hundred *li*,
he reached the kingdom of Kauśāmbī in Central India, which was six thousand *li* in circuit, with its capital city measuring over thirty *li* in circumference.
There are more than ten monasteries with over three hundred monks;
there are fifty deva temples with numerous non-Buddhist practitioners.
Within the city is the former palace and a great vihāra.
It is over sixty feet in height.
A sandalwood Buddha image is carved upon it, with a stone canopy suspended above;
this was created by King Udayana (also known as Udāyana, which in the language of Tang means "Born of Love").
A divine radiance flashed forth intermittently;
though the kings sought to lift it with all their might,
they were ultimately unable to move it.
Formerly, when the Buddha ascended to heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother,
the King requested Maudgalyāyana to employ his supernatural powers to escort artisans to heaven to model the Buddha’s features.
When the Buddha descended from heaven, the image immediately rose to welcome him.
The Buddha consoled and exhorted it, saying, "Only now shall you perform the work of a Buddha.
About one hundred paces to the east of the house [is where this occurred].
There are the footprints where the four Buddhas walked and sat.
The Buddha’s bathing well still provides water for drawing today.
In the southeast corner of the city is the residence of the householder Kuṭiśila.
There is a Buddhist vihāra containing a stūpa for hair and nail relics.
Beside that great stūpa, there are also the walking and sitting traces of four Buddhas. Nine li west of the city is a stone cave where the Buddha once stayed to subdue a venomous dragon.
To its side stands a great stupa over twenty zhang in height.
Beside it are the traces of the Buddha’s walking meditation as well as stupas for his hair and nail relics.
Those who seek cures for illness find recovery in many cases.
The Dharma bequeathed by Śākyamuni will perish in this country;
whether noble or humble, upon entering its borders, they are naturally moved to grief.
Traveling more than seven hundred li through the great forest to the northeast of the cave.
Crossing to the north bank of the Gaṅgā, one arrives at the city of Kāśapura,
which is approximately ten *li* in circuit.
This is the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla subdued the non-Buddhists.
The stupa is over twenty zhang in height.
The Buddha once preached the Dharma here for six months.
There are traces of his walking meditation as well as stupas containing his hair and nail relics.
Traveling northward for one hundred and eighty *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Viśoka. Central India is over four thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city is seventeen *li* in circuit.
There are twenty monasteries with three thousand monks.
There are fifty deva temples with a great multitude of non-Buddhist practitioners.
To the left and right of the road south of the city,
there are monasteries and stupas over twenty zhang in height.
The Buddha once preached the Dharma here for six years.
Beside it stands a marvelous tree seventy feet high, which does not change throughout spring and winter;
this is where the Buddha’s tooth-stick was discarded, yet it flourishes and grows.
Whenever those with wrong views come together to ravage and cut it down, it immediately grows back as before.
On its sides are the walking and sitting traces of four Buddhas, as well as stupas for their hair and nails;
the foundations of these corners connect one another, and the forest and ponds cast reflections upon each other.

From here, traveling northeast for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at Śrāvastī in Central India—this is the ancient city of Śrāvastī, with a circumference of over six thousand *li*; its capital city is now in ruins.
The foundations of the old site measure more than twenty *li* in circumference.
There are several hundred monasteries, but the number of monks is small.
There are over a hundred deva temples, and the non-Buddhists are very numerous. On the eastern foundation of an old palace in the desolate city stands a small stupa.
This is the site where King Prasenajit—formerly called Bosinide and translated into Chinese as Shengjun (Victorious Army)—built a hall for the Buddha;
the stupa stands upon the old foundations adjacent to it.
This is where the king built a vihāra for the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Prajāpatī (formerly called Po-she-po-ti; this means "Mistress of Beings"), a bhikṣuṇī.
To the east of that is a stūpa, which was the former residence of Sudatta (meaning "Good Giver").
To the side is a great stūpa;
this is where Aṅgulimāla—meaning "Finger-Garland"—abandoned his heterodoxy.
About six li south of the city is the Jetavana Grove.
This is the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden, a monastery built by the Crown Prince; it is now desolate, yet stone pillars still remain.
They were erected by King Aśoka and stand over seventy feet high.
One brick chamber remains, while the rest have been submerged and lost.
Inside the chamber is a golden statue of the Buddha preaching the Dharma for his mother;
to the northeast is a stupa commemorating the Buddha washing a sick monk;
and to the northwest is a stupa commemorating Maudgalyāyana lifting up the robe of Śāriputra.
Not far from it is a stupa at the site where the Buddha drew water for his use;
furthermore, there are stupas erected at the places where Śāriputra walked with the Buddha and preached the Dharma,
where divine medicines and extraordinary fragrances constantly descend.
Furthermore, a stupa was erected to mark the place where the non-Buddhists killed a girl in order to slander the Buddha.
One hundred paces to the east of the monastery is a large, deep pit.
This is the place where Devadatta, wishing to poison the Buddha, fell into a pit.
To the south is a great chasm;
this is the place where the bhikṣu Kokālika fell into a pit after slandering the Buddha.
Furthermore, eight hundred paces to the south is a large, deep pit,
the place where the Brahmin woman Cañcā fell alive after slandering the Buddha.
These three pits all penetrate through to the bottomless depths.

Torrential rains poured down incessantly without ceasing. Seventy paces to the east of the monastery was a vihāra named Yingfu (Shadow-Covering), sixty feet in height, containing a seated image facing east.
The Site for Debating with Non-Buddhists: To the east of this, the dimensions of the deva temple are equal to those of the vihāra.
On the first day, the shadow of the sun falling to the west did not cover the Buddha’s dwelling;
however, in the evening, the shadow falling to the east came to cover the deva temple.
Four li further to the east is the Great Dry Pond (Mahāśoṣa-taṭāka), the site where King Vīrasena—formerly called Liuli (琉璃)—sank into the earth.
Later generations erected a stūpa to commemorate this. There is also the place where Śāriputra competed with the non-Buddhists when he first founded the monastery.
He also erected a stūpa as a memorial.
Four *li* to the northwest of the monastery is the Forest of Attaining Sight (*Deyan-lin*),
within which is a stūpa marking the site where the Buddha walked.
When King Jayasena had gouged out the eyes of five hundred thieves,
he heard that through the Buddha’s power of compassion they were all restored at once;
he then abandoned his staff and gave rise to the heart of awakening.
Sixty li to the northwest of the city is an old city,
which was the birthplace of Kāśyapa Buddha when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years.
To its north is a stūpa, which marks the site where the entire bodily relics (śarīra) of this Buddha were enshrined;
King Aśoka constructed the stūpa to commemorate it. Furthermore, traveling southeast for more than five hundred li:

Upon arrival, [he found] the kingdom of Kapilavastu—formerly called Jialuopo in the old Indian language—which was over four thousand *li* in circuit. There were a dozen deserted cities, all of them uninhabited.
The palace city is approximately fifteen *li* in circumference and is constructed of brick; thus,
there are over a thousand temples, with one temple for every palace city.
There are more than thirty monks in the monastery.
There are two deva temples where various non-Buddhists reside.
Within the city, upon the foundations of the main hall:
Within the vihāra, there is an image of the King;
beside it, upon the foundation of the bedchamber of Queen Mahāmāyā— whose name means "Great Illusion"—
there is an image of the Queen fashioned within the vihāra.
In a vihāra at its side, there is an image of a Bodhisattva.
Regarding the signs of the deity’s descent, their interpretations differ.
The Sthavira school says:
According to the records of the Tang state, it was on the fifteenth day of the fifth month; other schools, however,
say it was on the eighth day of this same fifth month.
This is merely a difference between what has been heard and what has been seen.
To its side is the Xianxiang (Immortal’s Features) Stūpa;
to the south of the city is another stūpa.
This is the place where the Prince competed in strength and threw the elephant over the city wall so that it fell to the ground, forming a great pit.
Beside it is a vihāra containing images of the Prince and his teacher. Adjacent to that is a vihāra which was the chamber where the Queen resided.
[He] fashioned images of Yaśodharā and Rāhula. According to another version, it says:
"At the first watch of the night, the Prince opened the northern gate and departed.
Furthermore, [there is an image] in the vihāra at the southeast corner of the city."

The place where the Crown Prince, riding a white horse, leaped over the city walls into the air; at each of the four city gates there is a vihāra containing images of an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a śramaṇa.
Four *li* south of the city is the Nyagrodha Grove Stūpa.
This is the place where the Buddha attained the Way and preached the Dharma to devas and humans; it is the stupa within the old city, fifty *li* south of the present city.
This was the city of the Buddha Krakucchanda’s former birth when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years.
The stupa to the southeast of the city is the remains of this Buddha’s body.
King Aśoka erected a stone pillar more than thirty feet high in front of it.
Furthermore, about thirty li to the northeast, there is a stupa within the ruins of an old city.
When the human lifespan was forty thousand years,
this was the city of the birthplace of Kāśyapa Buddha.
To the northeast of the city is a stupa containing the remains of this Buddha.
King Aśoka erected a stone pillar to commemorate this event;
it is over twenty feet high. About forty li to the northeast of the city, there is a stupa at the site where the Prince sat beneath a tree.
To the northwest of the great city, there are several hundred thousand stupas;
these are the stupas for those who slew the Śākyaputras.
There were four Śākyaputras who resisted the army.
The people of the city did not accept him and he was expelled from the realm.
He became king of Udyāna once,
and king of Bamiyan and other regions three times.
To this day, [the tradition] has not ceased at the Nyagrodha-tree Stūpa south of the city,
which is the place where the Buddha first came to see his father, the King. The stūpa outside the southern city gate is the place where he competed in archery.
More than thirty li to the southeast,
this is where the Prince’s arrow struck the earth and caused a spring to gush forth.
Local tradition holds that drinking from this Arrow Spring cures many illnesses.
Alternatively, if one applies mud from it to the forehead, all suffering will be healed accordingly.
Furthermore, ninety *li* to the northeast lies the La-vani Forest,
where the bathing pools of the Śākya clan reflect the blossoming waters.
Twenty-five paces to its north is an *aśoka* tree, which is now withered;
this is the place where the Buddha was born. Some say:
Regarding this eighth day of the third month,
the Theravāda school says it corresponds to the fifteenth day of the third month. To the east, there is a stūpa at the place where the two nāgas bathed the Prince.
Immediately after his birth, the first Buddha walked seven paces in each of the four directions without support;
wherever he stepped, great lotus flowers emerged.
Having been born from the right side, the Lord of Devas received him with a robe.
The Four Kings received it and placed it upon a golden table.
In total, four stupas were erected and marked by stone pillars.
Beside them flows a small river toward the southeast.
It is popularly known as the Oil River.
After the Prince was born,
the heavens transformed this pool, making it radiant and lustrous so that he might be bathed therein.
Having cleared away the wind and the vacuity, it has now transformed into a river of water,
which remains as oily as oil.
From here, one travels east for more than two hundred li.
One arrives at a desolate forest within the kingdom of Rāmagrāma, where there are many empty cities in Central India;
to the southeast stands a Buddhist stūpa measuring less than one hundred feet.
In the past, this was one-eighth of the original relics.
A spiritual light frequently arose, and beside it was a clear pond where a dragon transformed into a snake and emerged to coil around the stupa.
Wild elephants gather flowers to scatter over it.
King Aśoka wished to open the *nāgārakṣita* [stūpa], but he was not permitted to do so.
Furthermore, about one hundred li to the east is a great stūpa in a large forest.

When the Crown Prince arrived here, he removed the maṇi jewels from within his precious robes and entrusted them to Cchandaka to return to his father, the King. To the east, there is a withered trunk of a Jambū tree that still remains.
There is a small stūpa at the place where the Prince exchanged his remaining garments for deer skin;
the stūpa beside it marks the place where he shaved his hair.
His age at that time was not fixed, though some say it was nineteen.
Twenty-ninth: Furthermore, traveling one hundred and ninety *li* southeast from here,
there is the Nyagrodha Forest Stūpa,
which is over three *zhang* in height.
In ancient times, people burned the ground at the Buddha's site and collected the remaining ashes and charcoal to erect a stupa here;
those who were ill prayed for recovery.
There are footprints where four Buddhas walked and sat;
the stupa is over a hundred feet high,
with several hundred small stupas to its left and right.
Furthermore, traveling northeast for five hundred li along a perilous mountain path,
one arrives at Kuśinagara, a city of Central India that is dilapidated and sparsely populated.
The stupa in the northeast corner of the inner city is the former residence of Cunda;
its well remains excellent, having been dug for the purpose of providing offerings.
It is four *li* to the northwest of the city.
He crossed the Aciravatī River—
this is translated as "Possessing Gold"—
and approached a śāla grove on the western bank.
The two groves were several dozen paces apart;
in their midst stood four trees that were exceptionally tall,
within which was a great brick vihāra.
An image of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa was fashioned,
lying with his head toward the north;
the adjacent stupa was over two hundred feet high.
In front stands a stone pillar inscribed with a record of the signs of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; it states:
"On the fifteenth day of the third month of this land."
The Sarvāstivādins say that it corresponds to the eighth day of the ninth month; however,
other schools hold differing opinions.
Up to the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era,
one thousand two hundred and twelve years had elapsed;
this is according to the stone pillar inscription at Bodhi Monastery.
Some say it has been one thousand three hundred years;
others say more than one thousand five hundred years.
Some say that since it has been more than nine hundred years but less than a thousand,
there is a Buddha statue beside the vihāra.
In the past, he was a king of pheasants who extinguished a fire, and a deer who saved a life;
stupas were erected for each of these deeds.
Next to the western stupa is the place where Subhadra—meaning "Virtuous" (Suxian) in Chinese—attained parinirvāṇa.
Next, there is a stupa at the place where the Vajrapāṇi deity prostrated himself on the ground.
Beside it is another stupa at the place where the coffin was kept for seven days. Beside that is another stupa at the place where Aniruddha ascended to heaven.
He informed his mother that she should come down to the place where he was weeping for the Buddha. Three hundred paces north of the city, across the Nairañjanā River,
is the stūpa marking the place where the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa*— the term *parinirvāṇa* meaning "to be cremated."
The ground here is now a mixture of yellow-black soil, ash, and charcoal;
those who offer prayers and receive a response all obtain śarīra relics.
Beside it is another stūpa, the place where the Buddha manifested his two feet for Mahākāśyapa.
Next, there is another stone pillar standing before a stūpa,
inscribed with a record of how the relics were divided among the eight kingdoms.
Traveling southwest from here for more than two hundred li, one arrives at a great city.

Furthermore, traveling over five hundred li through the Great Forest, he arrived at the kingdom of Vārāṇasī (formerly known as Kapilavastu), the ancient Pāṭaliputra of Central India. It was more than four thousand li in circuit; its capital city bordered the Gaṅgā River to the west.
It is over twenty *li* long and approximately six *li* wide.
The population is dense and prosperous, and most believe in non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*).
There are more than thirty monasteries with over three thousand monks, all belonging to the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are over one hundred deva temples and more than ten thousand followers of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika),
most of whom worship Maheśvara as their primary deity.
Within the great city, there are twenty deva temples.
The Heavenly Root (Devamūla) rises more than a hundred feet high.
To the northeast of the city is the River Vārāṇasī;
to its west is a stupa built by King Aśoka.
It stands over ten *zhang* high.
In front stands a stone pillar upon which green moss manifests the form of a Buddha. About ten *li* northeast of the river is the Ruru Monastery (*Luyesisi*).
Its precincts are divided into eight sections, enclosed by continuous walls and ramparts.
With its tiered eaves and multi-storied pavilions, there are fifteen hundred monks,
all belonging to the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There is a Buddha shrine more than twenty zhang in height.
The four sides of the brick niches contain hundreds of recessed figures,
including golden images and buddhas made of brass.
To the southwest is a stupa over one hundred feet high.
In front stands a stone pillar over seventy feet high;
it is transparently clear and pure, and through its sincere resonance, an image appears according to whether one's karma is good or evil.
Immediately after attaining enlightenment,
this was the place where he first turned the Wheel of Dharma; the three stupas beside it are the places where the three past Buddhas walked and sat.
Beside it are various stupas,
the place where five hundred pratyekabuddhas entered parinirvāṇa;
furthermore, there is another stupa at its side.
This is the place where the Bodhisattva Maitreya received his prediction of enlightenment.
Furthermore, one stupa to the west is where the Buddha, in a past life,
served as the Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
The place where Kāśyapa Buddha was prophesied to attain Buddhahood; next to it, southward, are the walking paths of four Buddhas,
fifty paces long and seven feet high,
constructed of piled blue stone, upon which are images of Śākyamuni in the posture of walking meditation.
The physical forms are exceptionally extraordinary, with the protuberance on the crown (uṣṇīṣa) and the hair-tuft (ūrṇā) standing out;
the hair emerges from the head with a divine and manifest character.
The traces of temples are extremely numerous, including viharas and stūpas.
These instances number in the hundreds and cannot be recorded in full.

To the west of the temple is a clear pond, two hundred paces in circumference, where the Buddha once bathed. Next to the west is a small pond where the Buddha once washed his utensils. North of that is another small pond where the Buddha once laundered his robes.
In the three ponds, dragons dwell; the water is sweet and pure.
Should anyone with arrogance touch it, the kumbhīra beast will immediately harm them.
Beside it is a square stone,
upon which are the imprints of the patterns of a Buddha’s monastic robe.
When fierce followers of external paths have stepped lightly upon them, [the marks would vanish].
The dragon of the pond frequently raises wind and rain.
Beside it stands a stupa;
it is said that the Buddha once manifested as a six-tusked elephant king there.
To the side [of the previous site] is another stūpa; it is the place where, because a hunter was wearing dharma robes, the Buddha extracted his teeth.

Furthermore, there is a stūpa in a great forest at the place where the Buddha, in a former life, was a bird and conversed with a monkey and an elephant regarding who was the greatest. There is also a stūpa in a great forest.
In the past, the Buddha and Devadatta were both deer kings.
The Buddha took the place of a pregnant doe to save her life;
it was from this that the name "Deer Park" (Mṛgadāva) originated. Three *li* to the southwest of the monastery...
The Great Stūpa is thirty *zhang* high; its foundation is imposing and magnificent.
Beside it is another stūpa, the site where the five men welcomed the Buddha.
The Stupa Three Li East of the Great Forest commemorates when the Buddha,
in a former life, was a hare; together with various beasts,
he knew his own body was too small, so he burned it to provide food for them.
Because he was moved to offer praise as the Lord of Devas descended,
a rabbit image appeared within the lunar disc.
To the east of the monastery, following the Ganges River for more than three hundred li.
To the east lies the kingdom of Zhanzhu (Jantuo), with a circumference of more than two thousand *li*.
Its capital borders the Gaṅgā River and measures over ten *li* in circuit.
The population is dense, and there are ten monasteries.
The monks number fewer than a thousand, all adhering to the Hīnayāna.
There are twenty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
To the northwest of the city is a monastery and stupa containing one *śīrṣa* (one *lǐng*) of the Buddha’s relics.
In the past, the Buddha preached the Dharma here for seven days.
There are also the walking and sitting traces of four Buddhas,
as well as an image of Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Though small in physical stature, his majestic virtue was great.
Over two hundred li to the northeast of the city, one reaches the Avīta-karṇa Monastery; it is said that the monks from the north do not pierce their ears because of this [circumstance].
Crossing the Gaṅgā River more than one hundred li southeast from the monastery, one arrives at a great city.
On the north bank of the river is a temple to the god Nārāyaṇa with a multi-storied pavilion that is most solemn.
Further thirty-odd li to the southeast is the Stūpa of the Subduer of Ghosts, half of which has already sunk into the ground.
In front stands a stone pillar over twenty feet high;
this is the place where the Buddha preached the Dharma for the sake of a man-eating ghost.
The ghost set up thousands of stone seats.
Lush forests and clear ponds are not far away;
several monasteries there are all inhabited by monks who study the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, crossing the river to the southeast for more than a hundred li, there is a stūpa.
This refers to the division of the relic casket and the remaining relics.
On every fast day, they emit light.
Furthermore, traveling one hundred and fifty *li* northeast across the Gaṅgā River, one arrives there.
Upon arrival, [he reached] Vaiśālī, which in ancient India was called Pi-shê-li; it is over fifty *li* in circuit.
Here, both heterodox and orthodox traditions are equally prevalent, and there are several hundred monasteries.
Currently, there are only fifty-three monks remaining;
there are several dozen deva temples, most of which consist of naked ascetics.
The city is already in ruins, its old foundations measuring approximately seventy *li* in circumference.
The palace city is approximately five li in circumference and is sparsely inhabited.
It is located six li to the northwest of the palace city.
The temple and stupa are the place where Vimalakīrti preached.

To the east is the stupa marking the site where Śāriputra realized the fruit [of arhatship]. Further to the east is the Great Stupa, which contains approximately one *hu* of the king’s share of the relics.
King Aśoka took nine *śu* and used them to uniformly construct the remaining stūpas.
Later, there was another king who wished to open [the stūpa].
The earthquake then ceased.
To the northwest stands a stone pillar supporting a stupa, six zhang in height.
Further south, a monkey dug a pond for the Buddha.
To the west of the pond is the place where a troop of monkeys held the Buddha’s almsbowl and climbed a tree to fetch honey; to the south of the pond is the place where the monkeys offered the honey.
Each site has a stupa as a memorial marker.
About four *li* to the northeast of the monastery is a stupa;
this is the site of the former residence of Vimalakīrti, where many numinous spirits still dwell.
His house was constructed of stacked bricks.
Tradition says it is Jishi (Accumulated Stone),
which is the place where the Dharma was preached while manifesting illness.
Recently, the envoy Wang Xuance measured it with his official tablet and found it to be only one zhang in length.
Thus, the name "Square Chamber" (fangzhang) originated from this;
it also includes the house of the Elder Ratnākara and the house of Āmrapālī.
At the place where the Buddha’s maternal aunt entered parinirvāṇa, monuments were erected for all [of them].
Four *li* north of the monastery is a stūpa at the site where devas and humans escorted the Buddha as he was about to depart for Kuśinagara. Next is another stūpa.
This is the site where the Buddha last gazed upon the city.
