within this, the first and last months may be extended or shortened as circumstances dictate.
Regarding the cultivation of the path, at what time would it not be appropriate?
Therefore, while the prohibition against wandering during the three periods of the day is universally established as an offense,
there are circumstances where one must attend to necessary affairs; in such cases, the principle of universal salvation is opened up,
provided that one does not become attached.
To the east of the Bodhi Tree Monastery, crossing the Nairañjanā River,
there is a pond to the north of a stūpa within the Great Forest.
This is where the Buddha, in a former life, was the son of a fragrant elephant.
Near where the mother of the blind elephant resided,
a stone pillar was erected.
In the past, Kāśyapa Buddha sat in meditative seclusion at this spot.
To the side are the walking and sitting traces of four Buddhas.
Within the grove is a small stone pillar;
this is the place where Udraka Rāmaputra made an evil vow.

Proceeding eastward again for more than one hundred *li* across the Mahā-aṭavī great forest wilderness, one reaches Mount Kukkuṭapāda—also called Kukkutapāda, meaning "Chicken's Foot," or Gurupāda, meaning "Venerable Foot. It rises directly upward with three peaks shaped like a chicken's foot.
Steep and precipitous, rising solitary and towering above the void;
its lower half covered by lush forests and its upper half by creeping vines—
this is where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa [resided].
It is named for the tranquil concentration within it.
The first Buddha bestowed upon Maitreya Buddha a golden-threaded *kāṣāya* robe woven by his maternal aunt.
He was to lead the fourfold assembly of disciples through the period of the Bequeathed Dharma.
Having received this mandate, twenty years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
Kāśyapa took up his robe and entered the mountains to await Maitreya.
Upon it stands a stupa;
when gazed upon during a quiet night, it illuminates itself like a bright torch.
It is located more than one hundred li northeast of Mount Kukkuṭapāda.
He arrived at Mount Buddhavana.
In a large stone cave on the northern cliff, the Buddha stayed for several years; nearby was a flat rock.
The sandalwood paste offered by Śakra Māra to the Buddha remains fragrant even now.
Traveling thirty-odd *li* east from the empty valley,
one reaches the Śiṃśapā Forest (also called the Daṇḍaka Forest), which fills the entire valley.
In the past, there was a man who attempted to measure the Buddha with a sixteen-foot bamboo staff;
however, the staff always extended beyond him.
Consequently, he threw down the staff and departed.
Consequently, roots grew there and covered the mountain.
In its center stands a stupa,
the site where the Buddha once preached the Dharma for seven days.
In the forest there was a lay devotee named Vijitasena,
who used scented powder as clay to fashion stupas five or six inches high,
upon which he inscribed scriptural texts; these were called "Dharma Relics."
For thirty years, day and night without slackening,
he fashioned seven hundred million small stūpas,
each one being placed inside a single large stūpa.
When the monks were invited for a Dharma assembly to celebrate these events, they all emitted radiance.
About ten li to the southwest of Yaṣṭivana,
on the sunny side of a great mountain, there are two hot springs that are extremely warm.
The Buddha transformed this place into a bathing pool;
those who came from near and far to bathe there all recovered from chronic illnesses.
Beside it are stupas containing images of the Buddha in the walking posture and Buddhist scriptures.
About seven li southeast of the forest,
atop a great mountain ridge, stands a stone stupa.
It was here that the Buddha preached the Dharma for gods and humans for two or three months.
King Bimbisāra piled stones to form a path,
twenty-odd paces wide and approximately four li long.
It is located about four li northeast of the Great Mountain.
One arrives at the hermitage of the Immortal on Mount Gu.
Five li further to the northeast is a small solitary mountain with a cliffside stone chamber capable of seating a thousand people;
it was here that the Buddha preached the Dharma for three months.
Upon a flat rock above the chamber, Brahmā and Śakra once applied sandalwood paste to the Buddha;
its fragrance remains potent even now.
In the southwest corner of the chamber is a rocky grotto.
This is the palace of the Asuras.
Beside the stone chamber is the plank path by which King Bimbisāra went to the Buddha’s dwelling;
it is a stone-paved road approximately five li in length, constructed as a flight of steps.
Traveling further east for more than sixty li, one arrives at the city of Kuśāgrapura, which means "City of Reed-Tops" or "City of the Reed Palace. This is the very center of Magadha.
The abundance of fragrant grass is the most excellent feature of this country.
Since ancient times, various kings have made their capitals on this mountain,
where the city gates and watchtowers still remain.
It is named after its fragrance.
A lofty mountain encircles it as an outer wall;
a narrow path leads westward, and a mountain gate opens to the north.
It is one hundred and fifty *li* in circumference from east to west.
The trees and flowers are lush and all are golden in color.
The inner city wall is over thirty *li* in circumference.
The city is desolate and utterly devoid of people. Outside the north gate is a stupa at the site where the Buddha extended his hand and manifested five lions,
subduing the intoxicated elephant Devadatta.
Furthermore, to the northeast is a stūpa,
which marks the place where Śāriputra heard the Dharma from the bhikṣu Aśvajit and realized the Path.
To the north of this stūpa is another stūpa beside a large, deep pit.
This is the place where Śrīgupta spoke of "superior honey" and prepared a fire pit to harm the Buddha;
there is a stūpa at the bend of the mountain city to the northeast of the pit.
This was the residence of Jīvaka, the King of Physicians.
A Dharma hall was built for the Buddha;
the surrounding walls and the flowering trees and fruit-bearing shrubs still remain.
The Buddha frequently stayed therein.
Fifteen *li* or so northeast of the palace city,
one reaches Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa— also called Vulture Peak or Vulture Terrace;
it is the ancient Ki-she-chü-chieh (Gṛdhrakūṭa) and adjoins the southern slope of the northern mountains.
Rising independently above the summit, it extends eastward and westward along the cliff edge.
On the western side hangs a brick chamber of extraordinary breadth and height;
its door opens to the east.
The Buddha dwelt in this world for fifty years and resided mostly in this chamber to preach the Dharma;
now, an image of his body, equal in size to the Buddha himself, has been fashioned here.
In the past, King Chāyāśubha, for the sake of hearing the Dharma,
traversed from mountain to peak, spanning valleys and scaling crags,
laying out stone steps for a path.
It is six *li* in circumference and over ten paces wide;
from the stone chamber at Yaṣṭivana to this point,
three stairways still remain.
Beside the steps are two small stupas:
one for the king to descend, and one to exclude ordinary people. Above them, there is a long stone to the east of the vihāra.
To the side where the Buddha once walked is a large rock, fourteen or fifteen feet high and over thirty paces wide;
this is the one hurled at the Buddha by Devadatta. Below the southern cliff is a stupa.
This is the place where the Buddha preached the Lotus Sūtra;
it is a great stone cave on the southern cliff of the monastery.
It was here that the Buddha entered meditative absorption.
In another room, Ānanda was terrified by Māra.
The Buddha reached through a stone wall with his hand and stroked his head;
a hole appeared where it had passed through.
To the northeast of the vihāra, at the Great Boulders of Daishikan,
is the place where the Buddha dried his robes;
its markings are now clearly visible.
Beside it is a footprint of the Buddha, its wheel-marked patterns engraved in stone.
On the summit of the northern mountain is a stupa;
from there, the Buddha gazed toward the city of Magadha.
The place where the Dharma was preached for seven days.
To the west of the north gate of the mountain city is Mount Vibhūṣaṇa.
On the shaded side of its southwestern cliff, there were formerly five hundred hot springs.
Even now, there are still several tens of them that partake of both warmth and cold.
Their source originates from the Anavatapta Lake on Mount Himavat, flowing out from its depths here.
They remain clear and delicious, identical in quality to their original lake.
Stone carvings were made of lion heads;
the stones flowed around below, where they were joined together to form a pool.
Those who bathed there were cured of their illnesses.
Monks at various monasteries take much of it to drink;
they wash their hair with it so that they remain perpetually pure throughout their lives.
The royal envoy Xuance once used it to wash his head.
Even after five years have passed, the hair remains constantly moist and pure, which is inconceivable. To the left and right of the spring, the foundations of stupas and monasteries stand in rows;
these are all the sites where the four Buddhas walked and sat.
Within this mountain, amidst a blend of forests and groves, lies a place frequented by recluses.
To the west of the spring is the Pipphala stone cave where the Buddha formerly resided constantly.
The cavern in the rear wall is the palace of the Asuras.
This stupa on Mount Vibhāra is the place where the Buddha preached the Dharma;
currently, naked ascetics (nirgranthas) reside there. It is located on the southern cliff’s shade to the left of the north gate of the mountain city.
About three *li* to the east is a large stone chamber, the place where Devadatta entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*). To the east of the chamber is a flat rock stained with blood;
in ancient times, there was a bhikṣu who practiced meditation here but did not attain realization.
He pierced his own neck and immediately realized arhatship.
On the cliff above is a stone stupa at the place where he ascended into the air, transformed into fire, and self-immolated;
it is also the place where those practicing meditative concentration threw themselves off the cliff to realize the fruit of enlightenment.
More than one *li* outside the north gate,
one arrives at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery.
It has a stone foundation and brick chambers opening toward the east.
The Buddha frequently stayed in this central hall, which still exists today.
Within it is a statue of the Buddha’s body; [it is located] at the Great Stūpa to the east of Zhuyuan.
This is the stūpa built by Ajātaśatru— also known as King Śaiśunāga—
who obtained a portion of the relics.
Later, King Aśoka opened it and constructed various other stūpas.
When others remain, it emits light.
To the side is the place where the Buddha walked for exercise.
To the east is the half-body stupa of Ānanda.
About six li to the southwest of Zhuyuan,
within a great bamboo grove on the northern side of the Southern Mountains, there is a large stone chamber.
This is where Mahākāśyapa and his thousand arhats resided.
At this site where the Tripiṭaka was compiled,
the Elder among the Saṃgha was immediately designated as the Sthavira, and thus the school became known as the Sthavira-vāda.
To the northwest of the chamber is a stūpa, which marks the place where Ānanda received reprimand and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
It is called the Stūpa of Realizing the Fruit.
Twenty-odd li to the west is a stūpa,
which is the place where the great assembly of those in training and those beyond training gathered to collect the five piṭakas.
It is for this reason that they are called the Mahāsāṃghika school. Over two hundred paces north of the Bamboo Grove is the Kalandaka Pond;
the Buddha frequently preached the Dharma here, but it is now dried up. About three li to the northwest of the pond is a stūpa.
The stūpa erected by King Aśoka stands sixty feet high;
the stone pillar is over fifty feet tall,
with the account of the stūpa’s erection inscribed upon it.
Not far to the northeast of the pillar, one reaches the city of Rājagṛha, which is the present-day Rājagṛha.
It was originally a forest region of Himavat;
it was built when King Śreṇika moved the capital there.
Four *li* to the northeast of the city of Māṇigrama, the outer wall has already collapsed.
The inner city is over twenty *li* in circumference,
with one gate on each side.
King Aśoka further established his capital at Gandhāra-pura (Xianghuacheng).
He brought these [images] as offerings to the brahmins;
those who reside there now number fewer than a thousand households. To the southwest of the palace city are two small temples.
This is the site where the Buddha formerly preached the Dharma;
many visiting monks from various countries came here to seek lodging.

Next, to the northwest, is the stupa at the old home of the elder Sudatta (also known as Jeta). This refers to the stupa on the left side of the road outside the south gate of the city of Śrāvastī, the King of Constellations.
This is the place where the Buddha preached the Dharma to ordain Rāhula.
Traveling further north for more than thirty li, one arrives at Nālandā Monastery;
it is said that this was originally the Amra Grove (Āmrapālīvana) donated by Śrīgupta.
In the past, five hundred merchants purchased it to offer as a gift to the Buddha.
Within it, the Dharma was preached for three months.
It was constructed through the combined efforts of five successive kings.
First was King Śakrāditya—
this means "Lord Sun"—
who founded this monastery.
Second is King Buddhagupta,
here translated as Juehu (覺護).
To the south of this, he built a monastery.
The third was King Cūdā-mādhava,
which means "Tathāgata" in this language;
next to the east, he built a monastery.
Fourth was King Brahmadatta,
which means "Illusory Sun.
Next, he built a monastery to the east.
The fifth is King Vaśala, which means "Vajra. To the north of this,
he constructed a monastery.
The surrounding walls stand high and steep, approximately five zhang in height.
There are seven courtyards in total;
each courtyard has three tiers and they share a single gate.
Throughout successive dynasties, its construction has reached the utmost in magnificence and splendor.
The monastery maintains strict regulations;
since its establishment, no women have ever entered.
Ten administrative officers inspect [the monastery] every evening.
Those who have not yet received full ordination are arranged in order according to their seniority.
There are several thousand monks.
There were nearly ten thousand renowned monks who traveled abroad to study;
most were men of exceptional talent and broad learning whose reputations resounded throughout foreign lands.
His followers numbered in the hundreds;
thus, all the monks of India looked up to him as their model.
There were none among them who did not discourse upon the essential meaning of the Tripiṭaka.
I feel ashamed of my own physical form.
Thus, when those from distant lands come to deliberate with me, the gatekeepers often interrogate them, causing many to be defeated and return.
Or, when visiting scholars of later generations engage in detailed discussions of their arts and talents, [the same occurs].
Those who have fallen from flight are surely seven or eight out of ten.
Thus, those of lofty talent, broad erudition, powerful memory, and many abilities,
possessing brilliant virtue that attracts others and joining with them in radiance as they engage with the world— [such figures are rare].
As for Dharmapāla and Candragupta, their achievements shook the fragrant dust of antiquity;
Guṇamati and Guṇavarmā spread their renown beyond the mundane world;
Prabhākaramitra’s pure discourse and Jayasena’s lofty talk [likewise remain celebrated].
The wisdom of Jñānacandra and the scholarly discipline of Śīlabhadra were both pure and sublime in their own time,
and their legacies have shone brightly throughout the ages.
Having mastered the ancient rites, he composed commentaries and exegeses totaling several dozen works,
which circulated widely during the era of prosperity;
thus, the sacred traces of this temple may be briefly recounted.
To the west of the monastery is a vihāra where the Buddha once preached the Dharma for three months.
One hundred paces further south is a small stūpa,
the site where monks from distant regions beheld the Buddha.
Furthermore, to the south stands a statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara;
some see him holding an incense burner and circumambulating the vihāra to the right.
Next to the south is a stūpa at the place where the Buddha once stayed for three months while shaving his hair.
Circumambulating it swiftly brings great healing.
The stupa by the side of the pond outside the western wall is the place where a non-Buddhist, holding a sparrow, questioned the Buddha.
More than fifty paces within the southeast wall,
there is a strange tree eight or nine feet high;
its trunk splits into two branches.
The Buddha’s discarded remains from his past chewing [of the tooth-stick] are still like this.

Next, to the east, is the Great Vihāra, over twenty *zhang* in height, where the Buddha once preached the Dharma for four months. Next, about a hundred paces to the north, is a vihāra containing an image of Avalokiteśvara.
Because their perceptions and feelings differ,
some stand by the side of the gate while others emerge before the eaves;
thus, both the state officials and the common people each offer their respective offerings.
Next is the Mahābodhi Vihāra, over thirty *zhang* in height.
King Śīlāditya constructed it with magnificent proportions;
its central Buddha image is identical to that in the vihāra beneath the Bodhi tree.
Next is the stupa in the northeast, the place where the Buddha once preached the Dharma for seven days; to the northwest is the place where the four Buddhas sat.
Next to the south is a brass vihāra, eighty feet high.
King Śīlāditya’s construction of it is still not yet finished.
Furthermore, more than two hundred paces to the east, outside the enclosure wall,
there is a standing bronze image eighty-odd feet in height.
The six-story pavilion was built by Prince Cao and is filled [with treasures].
Three li to the north, within a brick vihāra, is a statue of Bodhisattva Tārā; its dimensions are majestic and it is spiritually miraculous.
On the first day of the year, offerings are extensively prepared for it.
The kings, ministers, and subjects played various musical instruments for seven days before finally ceasing.
Within the gate of the monastery wall was a large well;
the Buddha [drew water] for a caravan of merchants suffering from heat and thirst.
Pointing to the ground, he said, "Water can be obtained here.
Thereupon, he struck the earth with the axle of his cart, whereupon a spring gushed forth; he drank from it and attained enlightenment.
About nine li southwest of the monastery is the site of Mṛgadāva’s former residence;
there, King Aśoka erected a stūpa to commemorate Maudgalyāyana. Furthermore, about four li to the east [of this site]...

This is the place where King Bimbisāra—here translated as Yǐngjiān (Shadow-Firm)—welcomed the Buddha. Furthermore, more than twenty li to the southeast is the stūpa built by King Ayodhya at the birthplace of Śāriputra.
Beside it stand the stupa of the Venerable One’s remains and a well.
Furthermore, five li to the southeast is a stupa where,
during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there were three hundred million great arhats.
At the same place where he entered nirvana, and some thirty-odd *li* further to the east, is the Cave of Śakra.
The cliffs and valleys are perilous, and the flowering groves grow tall and luxuriant.
Two peaks rise prominently, and on the southern face of the western cliff is a stone chamber.
The Buddha once stayed here.
Śakra drew forty-two points of doubt upon the rock to inquire about them;
their traces still remain.
Now, the images imitate those of the past;
upon entering, one’s reverence is solemn.
On the summit of the ridge are the traces of the four Buddhas walking and sitting.
On the Eastern Peak there is a temple.
At night, a monk looking westward saw lamps and torches burning before a stone chamber.
Before the temple on the Śakra Peak there is a stone pagoda; its origins are as related in the sutras.
About one hundred and sixty li northeast of Mount Di, one reaches the Kapota Monastery (meaning "pigeon" in Chinese). There are two hundred monks there.
To the east of the monastery is a stūpa.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for one night for the great assembly.
In the past, when the Buddha was a pigeon that threw itself into a fire to provide food for a hunter,
there was a stūpa of King Aśoka to the east.
Three *li* to the south of the stupa is a solitary mountain that is exceedingly high and precipitous.
It contains many stupas and temples; atop it is a statue of Avalokiteśvara, small in stature but great in majesty.
He holds a lotus flower in his hand and wears a Buddha image upon his crown.
Having fasted for seven days up to a month,
he beheld the true form emerge from within the image;
this was the vihāra originally built by King Saṃgharāja.
Traveling further southeast for forty li,
there is a monastery with fifty monks who study the Hīnayāna;
its great stūpa possesses many spiritual powers.
This is the place where the Buddha preached the Dharma for seven days to the Brahma Kings and others.
To its side are the footprints of four Buddhas, both walking and sitting. Over seventy li to the northeast of the monastery, south of the Gaṅgā River, lies [the site].
To the east of the deva temple is a great stūpa,
the site where the Buddha once stayed for one night and preached the Dharma. Proceeding further east into the mountain forests for over a hundred li,
there is a great monastery and a stūpa of King Aśoka.
Three *li* to the north is a great pond where the Buddha once preached the Dharma for three months;
it is over thirty *li* in circumference,
and lotus flowers of four colors bloom there throughout the four seasons.
Proceeding further east for two hundred li into the mountain forests,
one arrives at the country of Ilāṃvarta-bhadraka. Central India is more than three thousand li in circuit.
The northern side of the capital borders the Ganges River and is twenty *li* in circuit.
There are ten monasteries with more than four thousand monks;
most belong to the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are more than twenty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
Within the city are two monasteries, each housing fewer than a thousand monks;
both follow the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
On the side of the river north of the city is Mount Ilāṃtara,
where five-vidyā ṛṣis have resided since antiquity;
today there is a deva temple there.
The Buddha preached the Dharma here for three months.
To the south of the city is a stupa where the Buddha once preached the Dharma for three months.
Beside it are the traces of the walking and sitting of three Buddhas.
On the southern bank of the Ganges River, on the western border of the kingdom,
there is a solitary mountain over one li in length where the Buddha once observed the three-month rains retreat.
At the site where the yakṣa Kumbhīra was subdued, on a large rock at the base of the southeastern cliff,
there is the Buddha’s seated footprint, which has penetrated the stone by more than one cun;
it is five chi and two cun long and two chi and one cun wide.
Above it is a stūpa canopy.

To the south of that, on the stone, is the *kuṇḍikā*—that is, the water flask—of the Buddha; its base is over an inch deep and features eight-petaled flowers. Furthermore, to the southeast of the seated footprint is the footprint of a yakṣa.
It is sixteen inches long, eight inches wide, and two inches deep.
On the summit of the mountain is the chamber of a yakṣa.
To the north is the footprint of a standing Buddha, eighteen inches long, six inches wide, and half an inch deep.
To the west of the upper part of the stupa’s roof, there are six or seven hot springs that are extremely hot.
To the south of the country, in a great forest, there are many wild elephants of immense size.
From here, one follows the southern bank of the Ganges River.
Traveling three hundred li to the east,
one arrives at the kingdom of Campā in Central India, which is over four thousand li in circuit.
Its capital city borders the Ganges River to the north.
It is over forty li in circuit.
There are several tens of monasteries with more than two hundred monks, who study the Hīnayāna.
There are over twenty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
The city is built with brick walls several *zhang* high;
its defensive ramparts are lofty and steep.
At the beginning of the kalpa, when human beings first appeared, they lived in the wild, dwelling in caves.
Later, a celestial maiden descended among humans;
she went to the Ganges River to bathe and cleanse herself,
and being moved by its spiritual power, she conceived and gave birth to four sons.
He divided Jambudvīpa into territories and established cities;
this was the capital of his only son,
who was the first sovereign of Jambudvīpa.
The ground is warm and suitable for elephants.
One hundred and fifty *li* east of the city, south of the Ganges River, there is an isolated island surrounded by water;
on a mountain cliff in the center, many sacred shrines possess spiritual efficacy.
Wild elephants roam in herds throughout its borders.
Furthermore, traveling more than four hundred li to the east,
one arrives at...
The kingdom of Kajuṅghira, located in Central India, is over two thousand li in circuit.
There are seven monasteries with more than three hundred monks.
There are ten deva temples where followers of various heterodox schools dwell together.
The ground is largely marshy and damp.
To the north of the city, on the bank of the Gaṅgā River, there is a large, high terrace constructed of bricks;
its four sides are carved with images of Buddhas, devas, and others.
The southern border abounds in wild elephants; here, King Śīlāditya, while on a tour of inspection through Eastern India, constructed a temporary palace.
Furthermore, traveling eastward across the Gaṅgā River for more than six hundred li, one arrives [at this place].
Upon arrival,
[he reached] the kingdom of Bhoḍa (Bhōṭavaḍana) in Central India, which is over four thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city is over forty *li* in circuit and is densely populated.
There are more than twenty monasteries with over three thousand monks who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
There are about one hundred deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together; those who practice "naked asceticism" predominate.
To the west of the city, there are more than twenty major monasteries.
There are more than seven hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna;
it is from this region in East India that eminent monks emerge.
There is a stūpa of King Aśoka.
The Buddha once preached the Dharma here for three months;
on the day of the fast, he emitted light.
To the side are the traces of four Buddhas walking and sitting. Next, within the vihāra, there is an image of Avalokiteśvara.
Divine manifestations descend not only once;
many people have abstained from grain, and those who pray invariably receive a response.
The local terrain is low-lying and damp.
The Panasa fruit grows there;
it is both abundant and precious,
and as large as a crane's egg.
Or they may be found within tree branches and roots,
such as the *fuling* fungus.
Furthermore, traveling over nine hundred li to the east, one crosses a great river.
Arrival at the Kingdom of Kāmarūpa. It is located in Eastern India and is over ten thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city is over thirty *li* in circuit.
To this day, the Buddha-dharma has not yet appeared;
they personally serve the heavenly deities,
and there are several hundred temples dedicated to them.
There were several tens of thousands of followers of heterodox paths.
A Māra king named Tongzi (Child) occupied it;
they have inherited the rule for over a thousand generations.
The soil is springy and warm, and its people are prosperous and flourishing.
Its eastern border adjoins the southwest of the Tang;
it is said that various Man and Liao tribes from there pay tribute to the court.
It takes about two months to travel there,
at which point one enters the western border of Shu.
To the southeast of that country, wild elephants are also abundant.
When the king heard that the śramaṇa Xuanzang had come from afar to the Middle Kingdom,
he went out to welcome him and invited him to the east.
Upon meeting him, the king’s profound admiration was such that it felt as if they were old friends.
He inspired faith and became a light for the gates of the Śramaṇa community, illuminating the Buddha-dharma.
Xuanzang further subdued various non-Buddhists through debate,
leading them to receive the precepts of refuge and thereby spreading the transformative teachings even more widely.
Thus, the Buddhism of Eastern India was propagated by Xuanzang;
his renown resounded across distant frontiers until King Śīlāditya took notice of him.
Furthermore, when he was invited to return westward, the king again paid him the highest honors and respect.
The matter is recorded in a separate tradition.
From here, traveling south for one thousand three hundred li,
one arrives at...
The kingdom of Samataṭa is in Eastern India and is over three thousand *li* in circuit.
It is low-lying and damp near the sea.
The capital city is over twenty *li* in circuit.
There are more than thirty monasteries with over two thousand monks;
they belong to the Sthavira school.
There are more than a hundred deva temples where followers of heterodox paths, including those who go naked, are very numerous.
Beside the city is the Stūpa of King Aśoka,
the place where the Buddha once preached the Dharma for seven days;
nearby are the footprints of the four Buddhas, both walking and sitting.
In a temple to the side, there is a statue of green jade eight feet in height,
its marks fully and magnificently adorned. From here, traveling northeast along the coastal mountains and valleys of the great ocean,
lies the kingdom of Śrīkṣetra.
Next, in the southeast corner is the kingdom of Kāmarūpa; next to the east is the kingdom of Dvāravatī;
next to the east is the kingdom of Śrīpura; next to the east is the kingdom of Mahācampā.
This is the kingdom of Lâm-yìpí (Lin-yi). To the southwest of this is the kingdom of Yamunā-dvīpa.
These six kingdoms are all inaccessible due to the difficulties of the routes.
Furthermore, traveling nine hundred *li* west from the kingdom of Samataṭa, one arrives [at the next destination].
Upon arrival,
[he reached] the country of Dāmalipta in Eastern India, which is fifteen hundred *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is over ten *li* in circuit.
The coastal region is low-lying and damp.
There are ten monasteries with over a thousand monks,
and fifty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
The Stūpa erected by King Aśoka and the walking and sitting traces of the four Buddhas.
Traveling northwest again for more than seven hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Karṇasuvarṇa (Golden-Ear), which is in Eastern India. It is four thousand five hundred *li* in circuit.
The capital city is over twenty li in circuit.
Its population is dense and prosperous, with followers of both heterodox and orthodox teachings comprising about half each.
There are more than ten monasteries with over two thousand monks.
The Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school is present here;
there are more than fifty deva temples, and the number of heterodox sects is very great.
Separately, there are three monasteries that do not consume milk or curd; these belong to the Devadatta school.
Outside the city is a temple and stupa built by King Aśoka.
The Buddha once preached the Dharma here for seven days.
Beside it is a vihāra containing the traces of the four Buddhas walking and sitting.
Furthermore, traveling more than seven hundred li to the southwest,
one reaches the country of Oḍra in Eastern India; it is over seven thousand li in circuit.
The capital city is over twenty li in circuit.
There are more than one hundred Buddhist temples with over ten thousand monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna.
There are fifty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
There are more than ten stupas, all sites where the Buddha once preached the Dharma.
In the great mountains within the southwestern border,
there are many stone stupas at the Great Monastery that emit light on the day of the Great Fast (Rajja).
Beneath the dew-receiving basin, on top of the inverted bowl shape,
a flower-canopy shaft was placed and it remained fixed there,
just as a magnet attracts a needle.
From here, heading northwest to the mountain temple, the stupas differ while the temples remain the same as before.
These two stupas were constructed by spirits and ghosts. The eastern border borders the great ocean.
The city of Cīrāṭṭhā (Zhelidatuo) is said to be over twenty *li* in circuit.
It was here that merchants traveling by sea would halt on their journey.
Outside the city are five monasteries with lofty towers and pavilions, where the sacred images are exquisitely and uniquely crafted.
Traveling south for more than twenty thousand *li* from here across the sea, one reaches the kingdom of Siṃhala.

On a clear night, looking toward that Temple of the Buddha’s Tooth, one can see atop its spire, which rises several hundred feet, a *pāṭaligraha* jewel—its size being like a dry measure (*sheng*)—which is amber. The radiance of this pearl shines forth brilliantly, hanging like a lamp over this city.
Proceeding further southwest for over one thousand two hundred li through a great forest,
one arrives at the kingdom of Koṅgoda in East India, which is over one thousand li in circuit.
The city is more than twenty li in circuit and borders the sea.
The soil is hot and damp.
It abounds in rare treasures, such as conch shells, pearls, and great blue elephants.
The local customs believe in non-Buddhist paths;
there are one hundred deva temples and more than ten thousand followers of heterodox ways.
Within the territory, there are several dozen small towns situated along the mountains and seas.
Furthermore, to the southwest lies a vast wilderness forest;
traveling approximately fifteen hundred li, one reaches it.
Arrival at the Kingdom of Kalinga. Located in South India, it is over five thousand li in circuit.
The capital city is over twenty li in circuit.
They have little faith in the Buddha-dharma.
There are more than ten monasteries with over five hundred monks.
They belong to the Mahāyāna Sthavira school.
There are more than one hundred deva temples, and followers of various heterodox paths are very numerous.
South of the city is the Stūpa of King Aśoka, over one hundred feet high.
It contains the sites where the four Buddhas sat.
To the north of the border, atop a great mountain ridge, there is a stupa over one hundred feet high.
This is the place where a Pratyekabuddha entered parinirvāṇa at the beginning of the kalpa, when the human lifespan was immeasurable.
In the deep forests of the kingdom, extending for several hundred li, fragrant elephants emerge;
they are highly prized by neighboring states.
In the past, a seer possessing the five supernatural powers lived in a mountain cave, but when a person touched him, his spiritual powers receded.
He then used malevolent incantations to kill the people of this country;
even now, they are still few in number.
Furthermore, in the mountain forests to the northwest of here...
After traveling more than one thousand eight hundred *li*,
he arrived at the kingdom of Kauśala in Central India, which is more than six thousand *li* in circuit.
The mountain ridges encircle the region, with forests and marshes extending in succession.
The city is over forty li in circumference, with villages and hamlets facing one another.
The people have great faith in the Buddha-dharma.
There are more than one hundred monasteries with a population of nearly ten thousand monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna.
There are seventy deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
To the south of the city is an old monastery and stupa.
This is the place where the Buddha once manifested supernatural powers to subdue the non-Buddhists.
Later, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna resided in this monastery.
Furthermore, more than three hundred li to the southwest is Mount Balaramagiri, also known as "Black Bee. It rises toweringly and uniquely, its peaks steep and precipitous.
Since it has no cliffs or valleys, it resembles a single solid rock.
In ancient times, this country had a King Yinzheng (Yinzhengwang),
who, for the sake of a bodhisattva, excavated the mountain to construct a temple.
Several tens of *li* from the mountain, a tunnel was excavated;
directly beneath the mountain, one looks upward through a perforation in the rock.
There are long corridors with eaves, lofty terraces, and multi-storied pavilions.
The pavilion has five stories with four courtyards on each level;
its vihāras are all exquisitely crafted to the utmost degree of artistry.
From the summit of the mountain, cascading springs flow down in successive tiers, interconnecting one another.
As he bored through the hollows to draw forth light, the interior became transparent and radiant;
yet, once human strength was exhausted and his vital essence depleted,
his work remained half-finished, causing the King great anxiety.
Nāgārjuna secretly used divine elixirs to drip upon various large stones, causing them all to transform into gold.

Upon seeing this, the king was filled with joyful exultation and subsequently commissioned the construction of five tiers, in each of which he cast four great golden statues equal in size to the body of the Buddha.
The remaining stores were still accumulated in the treasury;
however, because there was a dispute among the monks, the laborers used up and scattered all the funds long ago.
Now, only the lay attendants (karmadāna) guard them, and their quantity is extremely large.
The caves were made so densely sealed that they could not be seen at all.
Furthermore, after the Dharma-treasury was bound,
it was forbidden for any of the sutras to be taken out from this mountain.
Recently, there have been those who cite medical prescriptions;
having entered [the fire] to treat illness, they emerge with their faces covered.
Consequently, those who succeed are rare.
Traveling over nine hundred li from Southern Forest,
one arrives at the country of Andhra in South India, which is more than three thousand li in circuit.
The capital city is over twenty li in circuit, containing twenty monasteries with more than three thousand monks.
There are over three thousand deva temples, and the non-Buddhists are extremely numerous.
Beside the city is a great monastery with multi-storied pavilions of extraordinary craftsmanship.
The Buddha images there also differ from those previously mentioned.
There is a stone stupa several hundred feet high,
which was built by an Arhat according to the instructions of Ajita.
More than twenty li to the southwest of the monastery, atop a solitary mountain ridge, stands a stone stupa;
this is the place where the Bodhisattva Dignāga composed the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*. Furthermore, one stupa lies to the southwest of that.
The Buddha once preached the Dharma here.
From this forest and wilderness, traveling south for more than a thousand *li*,
one arrives at...
The country of Dhānakataka is in South India and is over six thousand *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is over forty *li* in circuit.
Most of its monasteries have fallen into ruin; those that remain number more than twenty.
There are over a thousand monks,
belonging to the Mahāsāṃghika school.
There are over a hundred deva temples, and followers of various heterodox paths are very numerous.
The city lies between mountains to the east and west,
each of which has a great monastery.
In the past, the king carved away the stone and leveled the mountain for the Buddha.
It was constructed with extreme magnificence and breadth as a place for the sages and saints to dwell and rest.
Not long after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there were a thousand ordinary monks;
on the day their summer retreat concluded, they all realized the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Having ascended into the void and flown away, it is now silent and deserted.
There was the master of treatises Bhāviveka—translated here as "Clear Discernment"—who was the author of the *Prajñāpradīpa* (The Lamp of Wisdom).
Before Avalokiteśvara, he...
He abstained from grain and subsisted on water for three years,
awaiting the vision of Maitreya;
thereupon Avalokiteśvara manifested his physical body before him.
He commanded the Vajrapāṇi deity who dwells in the great mountain crag south of this city to recite the Vajra-mantra.
After three years, the deity granted him the instruction, saying:
"Within these rocky cliffs lies the palace of an asura."
If you make your request according to the Dharma,
the stone wall shall open and you may enter within;
wait for Maitreya to emerge, and I shall inform you.
After another three years, he recited mantras over mustard seeds and struck them against a stone wall; it suddenly burst open wide.
At that time, hundreds of thousands of people witnessed this and were filled with wonder and admiration.
The Master of Treatises stepped across the threshold and called out repeatedly for them to enter;
only six people followed him inside,
while the others regarded it as a den of venomous snakes.
Immediately, the stone gate closed back together like a wall.
From here, traveling southwest for more than a thousand li, one arrives at...
The country of Zhuliye (Caulika) is in South India and measures two thousand five hundred li in circuit.
Its capital city is over ten li in circuit.
The population is sparse, though there are some monasteries.
There are several dozen *nirgrantha* heretics at the deva temple.

To the east of the city is the Stūpa of King Aśoka, the place where the Buddha converted people and subdued the heretics. To the west of the city is the old monastery where the Bodhisattva Deva interrogated the Arhat Upatiṣya (translated here as "Superior"); after seven rounds of questioning, the Arhat remained silent and did not answer.
By the power of his supernormal faculties, he transported himself to the abode of Maitreya and said, "Devadatta is a Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa; you are not capable of competing with him.
In the time it takes to snap one's fingers, he returned and engaged in further discourse.
The Bodhisattva, knowing this, said to him:
"This is the explanation of the Great Sage Maitreya.
He traveled one thousand six hundred li through the wilds of the southern forest.
Arrival at the Kingdom of Draviḍa in South India. It is over six thousand li in circuit.
The capital city is over thirty li in circuit.
There are over one hundred monasteries with more than ten thousand monks,
all belonging to the Sthavira school.
There are also over eighty deva temples.
The Tīrthikas of the Many-Naked Form school have a stūpa of King Aśoka here;
the Buddha frequently visited this place to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings.
The stupa of the Great Monastery to the south of the city is over one hundred feet high;
it is the place where the Buddha once preached the Dharma and subdued the non-Buddhists.
There are also the walking and sitting traces of the four Buddhas.
From here, traveling south for more than three thousand *li*,
one arrives at the country of Malakūṭa in South India, which is over five thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city is approximately forty li in circuit.
The monks are few,
while there are several hundred deva temples and a great many naked heretics.
The soil there is saline and barren, so vegetation does not flourish.
To the east of the city is the temple of King Aśoka’s younger brother;
furthermore, King Aśoka erected a stupa there.
The Buddha once taught that prayers for the fulfillment of one's aspirations would all be granted.
To the south of the kingdom, near the sea, there is Mount Mukhaliya,
where white sandalwood trees grow.
Furthermore, the karpūra tree has a trunk like that of a pine but different leaves;
its fragrance is like ice and snow,
which is the camphor incense (nāgakesara).
In Shandong there is Mount Potalaka.
At its summit is a lake from which a river flows down and becomes a great river;
it circles the mountain thirty times before entering the South Sea.
The celestial palace by the side of the pond is the dwelling place where Avalokiteśvara roams;
those who pray there perceive him in the form of the deity Maheśvara.
To the east of the mountain, on the northern shore of the sea, lies the city of the ancient kingdom of Siṃhala, which is now more than three thousand li from the coast.
It reaches the country of Siṃhala, which is not included within India; it is what is called Sīhaḷa. It is over seven thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city is over forty *li* in circuit, and its population is extremely prosperous.
The monastery houses several hundred monks and more than twenty thousand people;
it belongs to the Theravāda school. Beside the palace is the Tooth Relic Shrine (Dantadhātu-cetiya), which is as high and broad as the one previously described.
In the palace, eighteen thousand monks were provided with daily meals;
this practice was only recently abolished due to civil unrest over the past decade or so.
Within a small shrine beside the Tooth Relic, there is [a record].
On the uṣṇīṣa of this seated statue made of gold and copper, a rare jewel was set.
In the past, a person, upon bowing before it, saw the jewel and gave rise to greed;
he stole it that night, but did not reach the head of the statue.
He then said, "In the past, the Buddha valued his life lightly for the sake of living beings; why now are you so stingy with this treasure?
Thereupon, the image bowed its head and gave it to him.
Later, the king learned of this but did not punish him;
he ransomed the jewels and returned them to be placed atop the image’s head.
To this day, the image keeps its head bowed.
Several thousand li from the southeastern corner of the country lies the island of Nalaka.

Its inhabitants are three feet tall, have bird-like beaks, and subsist solely on coconuts. At the southeastern corner of this country and island is Mount Lika, a place frequented by spirits and deities.
The Buddha preached this sutra here.
Several thousand li by sea to the west of the continent,
on the eastern cliff of a solitary island, there is a stone Buddha over one hundred feet high.
Sitting facing east, he has a *cūḍā* (cranial protuberance) made of moon-love jewels (*candrakānta-maṇi*).
When the moon is about to turn its light back to shine upon him,
water flows down in suspension, which people then consume.
To the west of the continent, floating upon the sea for several thousand *li*, there is a Great Treasure Island (*Mahāratnadvīpa*).
No one dwells there, and no one has ever reached it.
Furthermore, traveling more than two thousand *li* north of the forest in the kingdom of Daradvīpa:
Upon arrival,
[he reached] the country of Koṅkaṇapura in South India, which is over five thousand li in circuit.
The capital city is over thirty li in circuit.
There are over one hundred monasteries with more than ten thousand monks,
who study both the Mahayana and Hinayana traditions.
There are several hundred deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
To the side of the palace is the Great Temple Monastery, over ten *zhang* in height,
with more than three hundred monks residing there.
Among its treasures is the precious crown of Prince Sarvārthasiddha.
It is about two chi shorter [than the previous].
On fast days it emits light;
this was the time of the Bodhisattva. Within the great monastery beside the large city, there is a shrine more than five zhang in height.
Two hundred billion arhats are said to have been created by this one person as images of Maitreya Bodhisattva;
they are over ten feet high and emit light on days of fasting.
To the north of the city, near the Tāla Grove, there is a perimeter of more than thirty li.
The leaves are broad and long, their color lustrous and smooth;
they are harvested by various nations alike to serve as writing material.
Within the grove are stupas marking the walking and sitting traces of the four Buddhas.
There are also two billion stūpas containing śarīra relics within this grove, to the east of the city;
these stūpas are thirty feet high and emit light on the days of the śarīra fast.
The Buddha once traveled here to preach the Dharma.
Furthermore, about two thousand five hundred li to the northwest lies a forest inhabited by fierce beasts.
Upon reaching the country of Mahārāṣṭra in South India, it is more than six thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city borders a great river and is over thirty *li* in circuit.
Its customs dictate that kindness must always be repaid and enmity must always be avenged.
The powerful and arrogant [ruler] was not subject to King Śīlāditya.
There were more than one hundred monks in the monastery, numbering over five thousand, who studied both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
There were also several hundred deva temples, with a vast multitude of followers of heterodox paths.
Within and outside the great city are the walking and sitting traces of five stupas and four Buddhas,
which King Aśoka marked with monuments.
To the south of the city, in an old temple, there is a stone image of Avalokiteśvara.
It was built by an arhat at Dàshān Temple on the eastern frontier in the hope of attaining many fruits [of merit].
The Great Vihāra is over one hundred feet in height.
The stone statue is over seventy feet high.
Above it are seven tiers of stone canopies,
suspended in mid-air with each tier separated from the next by three feet.
The tradition states that this is sustained by the power of the Arhats' vows,
or by their majestic spiritual power, or by the power of medicinal arts;
thus, various explanations differ.
On all four sides of the vihāra,
there are carved depictions of the Buddha’s stages on the path to enlightenment, his realization of the fruit, and his entry into parinirvāṇa,
complete in every detail. Outside the temple gate, to the south and north...
There is a stone elephant at each [gate].

Tradition says that when the elephant roars, the earth trembles. From here, traveling west for more than a thousand *li*, one crosses the Narmadā River and arrives at the kingdom of Valabhī (Bālūjiēchìpó), in South India, which is two thousand five hundred *li* in circuit.
The capital city is over twenty li in circuit.
Heretics and those of the orthodox faith both have faith there.
There are more than ten monasteries with over three hundred monks.
They study the Mahāyāna and the Sthavira school.
There are ten deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
The soil is saline and poor, and vegetation is sparse and thin.
From here, traveling northwest for more than two thousand li,
one arrives at the country of Mālava in South India, which is over six thousand li in circuit.
The capital city is over thirty li in circuit and is situated along the Mahī River;
its southeastern region is a place where the five Indias value learning.
The people are naturally kind and compliant, a quality not found in other countries.
Together with Magadha in Jambudvīpa,
there are only these two countries that revere the Teaching;
they both place their faith in both the heterodox and the orthodox.
There are several hundred monasteries with more than twenty thousand monks,
belonging to the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are also several hundred deva temples.
Those who follow heterodox paths smear their bodies with ash,
and their followers are numerous. Twenty li to the northwest of the city is a large settlement of Brahmins.
Beside it is a great pit whose flowing waters never fill.
This is the place where, in the past, the arrogant Brahmin who slandered the Mahāyāna fell into hell.
From here, one enters the sea route to the southwest.
Traveling again northwest for more than two thousand five hundred li,
one arrives at...
The country of Aṭali is in South India and is more than six thousand *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is over twenty *li* in circuit.
The population is dense and prosperous; the people serve the heavenly deities.
There are more than ten shrines where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
The soil is sandy and saline;
it produces pepper trees that resemble those of the Sichuan pepper.
Furthermore, *kunkuma* incense is produced there;
its leaves resemble those of the *táng* tree.
Moreover, traveling northwest from the country of Malaya for three days, one hundred *li* constitutes a day’s journey.
Upon reaching the kingdom of Kheṭa in South India, it is over three thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city is over twenty *li* in circuit and is densely populated.
There are more than ten monasteries with over one thousand monks.
Both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings are studied there;
there are several dozen deva temples, among which the followers of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas) are particularly numerous.
Furthermore, traveling north for more than a thousand li:
Arrival at the Kingdom of Valabhī. Located in South India, it is a branch of North Lāṭa.
It is over six thousand *li* in circuit, and its capital city is over thirty *li* in circuit.
The population is dense and numerous;
there are several hundred households possessing wealth of one billion coins.
There are over one hundred monasteries with more than six thousand monks.
There are many hundreds of deva temples belonging to the Haimavata school of the Śrāvakayāna, and there are also many non-Buddhists.
The Buddha frequently traveled to this country,
and King Aśoka erected many stūpas here.
There are footprints where three Buddhas walked and sat. Furthermore, traveling over seven hundred li to the northwest,
one arrives at the country of Ānandapura in Western India, which is over two thousand li in circuit.
The capital city is over twenty li in circuit;
its households are numerous,
and there are more than ten monasteries with fewer than a thousand monks.
The Sammitīya school of the Hīnayāna is present here;
there are several dozen deva temples where various non-Buddhists dwell together.
From Valabhī, it is more than five hundred li to the west.
Upon arrival in the kingdom of Surāṣṭra in Western India, it was found to be over four thousand *li* in circuit, with its capital city measuring over thirty *li* in circumference.
To the west, it borders the Mahī River.
The inhabitants of Pūrṇaśālā follow both heterodox and orthodox teachings;
there are over fifty monasteries with more than three thousand monks.
It is also of the Theravāda school.
There are over a hundred deva temples where various non-Buddhists dwell together.
The soil is saline and barren, and flowers and fruits are scarce.
The country is not far from the mouth of the Western Sea.
On the summit of a mountain to the west of the city there is a monastery,
vast, spacious, magnificent, and beautiful, where immortals and sages dwell.
Traveling again from Valabhī for more than one thousand eight hundred *li*,
one arrives at the country of Gurjara in Western India, which is more than five thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city is over thirty li in circuit.
The people are generally lacking in faith.
There is one Buddhist monastery with one hundred monks.
The Hīnayāna teachings are studied here,
and there are several dozen deva temples with many followers of heterodox paths.
Furthermore, traveling more than two thousand eight hundred li to the southeast:
Upon arrival,
[he reached] the country of Oḍra (Ujjayanī) in South India, which is more than six thousand *li* in circuit;
its capital city is over thirty *li* in circuit.
The population is dense.
There are five monasteries in existence,
with three hundred monks.
Both Mahayana and Hinayana teachings are studied there;
there are several dozen deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
The soil is salty and fruit is scarce.
The stupa by the side of the city marks the place where Aśoka established a hell.
Furthermore, traveling over a thousand li to the east:
Upon arrival,
[he reached] the kingdom of Citra in South India, which is over four thousand *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is approximately fifteen *li* in circumference.
There are several tens of monasteries with few monks.
There are ten deva temples with over a thousand non-Buddhist practitioners.
Furthermore, traveling north for more than nine hundred li:
Upon arrival,
[he reached] the kingdom of Maheshvarapura in Central India, which is three thousand li in circuit.
The capital city is over twenty li in circuit.
They do not believe in the Buddha-dharma.
There are several dozen deva temples belonging to the ash-smearing heretics.
Traveling approximately two thousand li northwest from the wilds of Kukkurā,
one crosses the Indus River and arrives [at the destination].
The country of Sindhu, located in Western India, is over seven thousand *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is more than thirty *li* in circumference.
The soil produces gold, silver, and brass.
One peak has a very small camel that produces red, white, and black salt.
There are several hundred Buddhist temples with more than ten thousand monks.
It also follows the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna,
yet its practitioners are mostly indolent.
There are thirty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.

The Buddha frequently traveled here, and King Yù erected several tens of stūpas. Alongside the Wū River, for over a thousand *lǐ*, there are hundreds of thousands of households amidst marshes and wetlands;
they take up cattle herding as their livelihood and are solely devoted to slaughter.
There is no distinction between noble and base, male and female, or monastic and lay;
yet they shave their hair, don the *kāṣāya*,
and in outward form resemble *bhikṣus*, while delighting in vulgar and worldly conduct.
Furthermore, harboring narrow views, they rejected the Mahāyāna.
Formerly, there was an Arhat who traveled through the air to convert them;
having bestowed upon them the Three Refuges, he ordained them and had them practice the Dharma.
This is because they later returned to their original customs.
From here, traveling east for over nine hundred li,
one crosses to the eastern bank of the Indus River.
Arrival at the Kingdom of Morasatpura. Located in Western India, it is four thousand li in circuit.
The capital city is over thirty li in circuit.
The people all belong to the kingdom of Takka.
There are more than ten monasteries, but the monks are extremely few.
They have particular faith in celestial deities, of which there are eight shrines.
There are many non-Buddhist practitioners.
Beside the city is a temple of the Sun God (Sūrya), which is most magnificently adorned; the form of the deity is cast in gold.
It was adorned with rare treasures, and female musicians performed in turn.
Surrounding it were magnificent lotus ponds and lush, beautiful groves.
Here, the kings of the five regions of India established houses of merit.
He distributed goods to those who were poor and sick.
Furthermore, traveling over seven hundred li to the northeast,
he arrived at...
The country of Pārvatī is a dependency of Takka in North India;
it is over five thousand *li* in circuit, and its capital city is over twenty *li* in circuit.
The people all have mixed religious beliefs.
There are more than ten monasteries with over a thousand monks;
they study both the Mahayana and Hinayana teachings.
There is a stupa of King Aśoka.
There are twenty deva temples.
Beside the city is a great monastery with over a hundred monks,
all of whom study the Mahāyāna.
It is frequently struck by lightning and burned by fire.
The soil is rich in dry-rice (śāli).
It is one thousand six hundred li southwest from the Sindhu River.
Arrival at Āndhrabhṛtya. This country of West India is five thousand li in circuit.
The capital city is over thirty li in circuit.
Situated in a remote western region and on low-lying ground,
it borders the Indus River and adjoins the great ocean.
It reveres the Buddha-dharma, possessing more than eighty monasteries with over five thousand monks.
There are many followers of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are ten deva temples belonging to the ash-smearing heretics (Pāśupatas).
The Buddha once traveled here; King Aśoka erected six stūpas at this site.
Furthermore, two thousand li less than the western city,
